Anton menjawab tanpa perlu membuka catatan — tanda ia sudah menghafalnya. “Nusa Tenggara Barat dan Timur, Bu. Yang selama ini memiliki angka pernikahan dini tertinggi secara nasional. Di sana penurunannya dua puluh tiga persen.”

“Implementasi di sana tidak mudah,” Angel menambahkan. “Ada resistensi adat yang sangat kuat di awal. Tapi tokoh-tokoh adat yang akhirnya mau duduk bersama kita — ada tiga atau empat orang yang benar-benar mengubah arah narasi di komunitas mereka.”
Nisa mengangguk. “Nama mereka sudah dicatat?”
“Sudah, Bu. Ada dalam lampiran laporan.”

“Saya mau ada penghargaan formal untuk mereka tahun ini. Bukan dari Kementerian, bukan dari DPR. Dari kantor Presiden langsung.” Nisa menoleh ke Angel. “Sesuatu yang personal. Bukan sekadar plakat dan foto.”
Angel mencatat. “Siap, Bu.”
Reza, yang duduk di sofa sudut ruangan dengan secangkir kopi dan buku yang sudah sejak tadi tidak benar-benar ia baca, mengangkat pandangannya. “KDRT-nya?”

“Turun dua puluh dua persen laporan yang masuk,” Anton menjawab. “Tapi yang lebih penting — akses layanan bantuan hukum naik tiga ratus persen. Artinya bukan korban yang berkurang, tapi yang akhirnya berani melapor dan mendapat bantuan yang meningkat pesat.”
Reza mengangguk pelan. “Itu yang lebih penting.”
“Jauh lebih penting,” Nisa setuju.

Ada keheningan yang nyaman di ruangan itu — keheningan empat orang yang sudah cukup lama bekerja bersama untuk tidak perlu mengisi setiap jeda, yang tahu bahwa diam kadang adalah cara terbaik untuk membiarkan sesuatu yang baru saja disampaikan meresap sepenuhnya.

“Masih banyak yang belum beres,” Nisa akhirnya berkata. Bukan sebagai pesimisme — sebagai fakta yang ia terima dengan tenang. “Resistensi di beberapa kabupaten masih tinggi. Anggaran implementasi di daerah 3T masih jauh dari ideal. Tenaga konselor yang terlatih masih kurang.” Matanya memindai ruangan. “Ini bukan saatnya puas.”
“Tapi?” Angel sudah tahu pola bicara Nisa cukup baik untuk tahu ada tapi.
Nisa tersenyum tipis. “Tapi arahnya jelas. Dan itu — setelah semua yang kita lalui — itu bukan hal kecil.”
Perayaan kecil itu terjadi bukan karena direncanakan.

Sore itu, setelah Angel dan Anton pergi, Nisa menemukan Reza masih di sofa yang sama, tapi bukunya sudah ditutup. Di atas meja kecil di sampingnya ada dua cangkir — kopi Gayo untuk dirinya, teh melati untuk Nisa — dan sebuah kotak kecil dari patisserie langganan mereka.
“Apa ini?” tanya Nisa.
“Donat cokelat meses.” Reza membuka kotaknya dengan cara seseorang yang sudah menyimpan sesuatu dan sangat puas dengan dirinya sendiri. “Yang kamu bilang tidak sempat kamu makan sejak… entah kapan.”
Nisa menatap kotak itu. Menatap Reza.
“Za, ini—”
“Bukan perayaan besar,” potong Reza. “Hanya donat. Dan dua orang yang layak makan donat setelah empat tahun.”
Nisa duduk di sebelahnya.
Mengambil satu donat. Menggigit. Matanya memejam sedetik — bukan drama, tapi tulus, cara seseorang yang baru menyadari betapa lama ia tidak melakukan hal sesederhana ini.
“Reza.”
“Hm?”
“Ini memang enak banget.”
Reza tertawa — tawa yang dalam dan nyata, tawa seseorang yang tidak punya agenda lain selain momen ini.
“Iya,” katanya. “Kataku juga dari dulu.”

Mereka makan donat di sofa ruang kerja Presiden Republik Indonesia di sore yang biasa — tanpa kamera, tanpa agenda, tanpa siapa pun yang tahu kecuali Mas Anto yang berdiri di luar pintu dan sudah sangat terlatih untuk tidak pernah menceritakan hal-hal seperti ini kepada siapa pun.
Dua orang yang sudah cukup lama bersama untuk tahu bahwa kebahagiaan sejati tidak pernah butuh penonton.
Di luar jendela, Jakarta bergerak dengan cara Jakarta selalu bergerak — tanpa henti, tanpa meminta izin, tanpa peduli pada apa yang baru saja diselesaikan atau apa yang masih menunggu untuk dimulai.
Tapi di sofa itu, untuk dua puluh menit yang tidak akan pernah muncul di berita mana pun — ada cahaya.
Bukan cahaya yang menyilaukan. Bukan cahaya yang butuh diumumkan.
Cahaya kecil yang hangat dan stabil.
Yang paling susah didapat, dan yang paling berharga untuk disimpan.
— Selesai, Bab 24 —
ISTANA PENUH BARA

chapters.heading: Epilog: Harmoni Bangsa
paragraphs: Balkon Paviliun Pribadi Presiden, Istana Negara
30 Oktober 2048
Dua puluh tiga tahun.

Hari ini, dua puluh tiga tahun yang lalu, Nisa Shabrina Farha dan Reza Satria berdiri di depan penghulu dengan tangan yang sedikit gemetar dan senyum yang tidak tahu bagaimana cara menyembunyikan kegugupannya. Tidak ada yang hadir hari itu yang menduga bahwa pasangan muda itu akan berakhir di sini — di Istana Negara, di balkon ini, di bawah langit Jakarta yang malam ini memilih untuk bersikap lebih indah dari biasanya.
Atau mungkin langitnya sama saja. Hanya cara memandangnya yang sudah berubah.
Tidak ada konferensi pers hari ini.

Nisa memutuskan itu sejak awal Oktober — anniversary ke-23 adalah milik mereka, bukan milik publik. Cukup sudah tahun-tahun sebelumnya dengan blitz kamera dan pertanyaan tentang rahasia pernikahan yang awet. Tahun ini, cukup mereka berdua. Dan Alex, yang terbang pulang dari Jerman khusus untuk tiga hari.

Alex yang sudah dua puluh tahun, yang tingginya sekarang definitif melampaui Reza dan tidak pernah berhenti mengingatkan hal itu, yang aksen Jawa-nya sekarang bercampur dengan aksen Jerman-Inggris yang lucu, yang sudah tidur dua belas jam sejak landing kemarin karena jet lag yang ia dramatisasi lebih dari yang perlu.
Malam turun dengan tenang.

Di taman paviliun di bawah balkon mereka, lampu-lampu kecil yang sudah Reza pasang sejak sore berkilauan di antara dedaunan. Bukan lampu yang sama dengan yang dipasang untuk pesta ulang tahun Nisa tiga tahun lalu — lebih sederhana, lebih personal. Hanya beberapa ratus titik cahaya kecil yang menciptakan suasana yang tidak butuh kata-kata untuk dijelaskan.

Di atas meja teras: dua gelas jus apel. Satu kotak kecil dari patisserie langganan — kue cokelat truffle, bukan kue perayaan yang megah. Dan sebuah pemutar musik portabel kecil yang sudah Reza sambungkan sejak tadi, playlist-nya sudah siap.
Nisa berdiri di railing balkon, menatap kota di bawahnya.

Jakarta di malam hari — jutaan cahaya yang tidak pernah sepenuhnya padam, denyut sebuah kota yang terlalu hidup untuk tidur. Ia sudah menatap pemandangan ini ratusan kali dari balkon yang sama, dari momen-momen yang sangat berbeda satu sama lain.
Malam-malam ketika ia berdiri sendirian dengan pertanyaan yang tidak punya jawaban.
Malam-malam ketika Reza berdiri di sampingnya dan pertanyaan-pertanyaan itu terasa lebih ringan hanya karena ada seseorang yang mau menanggungnya bersama.
Malam ini.
Yang terasa — berbeda dari semuanya.
Reza muncul dari pintu balkon, membawa dua gelas jus apel. Meletakkan satu di tangan Nisa yang sudah teruluir secara otomatis, dan berdiri di sampingnya.
“Alex sudah tidur lagi?” tanya Nisa.
“Di sofa. Sambil pegang remote TV.” Reza menyesap jusnya. “Tidak sampai tiga menit tadi.”
Nisa terkikik. “Masih sama seperti dulu. Kalau tidak sengaja ketiduran, bukan Alex namanya.”
Keheningan yang nyaman turun di antara mereka.

Bukan keheningan yang perlu diisi. Jenis keheningan yang sudah sangat mereka kenal — keheningan yang muncul ketika dua orang sudah cukup lama bersama untuk tahu bahwa kehadiran bisa berbicara lebih keras dari kata-kata.
Di bawah, taman paviliun berkilauan dalam cahaya kecil-kecil yang hangat.
Reza mengambil pemutar musik dari meja teras. Menekan play.
Yang keluar bukan Miles Davis atau Earth Wind & Fire atau The Corrs.

Yang keluar adalah sesuatu yang berbeda — sebuah komposisi instrumental yang Nisa tidak langsung kenali. Melodinya mengalir dengan cara yang terasa seperti perpaduan: ada sentuhan ambient yang tenang, ada melodi sederhana yang sedikit terasa seperti fiddle Irlandia, ada ketukan yang hampir tidak terasa tapi ada.
“Ini apa?” tanya Nisa.
Reza senyum. “Buatanku.”
Nisa menoleh. “Kapan?”

“Pelan-pelan. Selama beberapa bulan terakhir.” Ia menatap pemutar musik di tangannya. “Waktu aku mulai belajar lagi di studio kecil itu. Campuran dari musik yang kita masing-masing suka — ambient-nya dari aku, melodinya terinspirasi dari The Corrs yang kamu suka.” Senyumnya sedikit malu, cara yang jarang sekali ia tunjukkan. “Belum sempurna. Tapi aku pikir, malam ini adalah waktu yang tepat untuk pertama kali diputar.”
Nisa mendengarkan.
Benar-benar mendengarkan — bukan dengan telinga yang sedang memproses informasi, tapi dengan cara mendengarkan yang lebih tua dari itu.
Melodi itu mengalir. Sederhana, tidak kompleks, tapi punya kedalaman yang hanya muncul dari sesuatu yang dibuat bukan untuk didengar banyak orang tapi untuk satu orang saja. Atau dua.
“Za,” kata Nisa pelan.
“Hm?”
“Ini indah.”
Reza tidak menjawab. Hanya mengulurkan tangannya.

Nisa menyambutnya — jemari bertautan dengan cara yang sudah dua puluh tiga tahun menjadi memori otot, cara yang tidak pernah perlu dipikir tapi selalu terasa seperti pulang ke tempat yang paling tepat.
Mereka berdiri seperti itu cukup lama, membiarkan melodi itu mengisi udara malam yang segar, membiarkan Jakarta terus berdenyut di bawah mereka.
“Kamu sudah memutuskan?” tanya Reza akhirnya. Nada suaranya ringan, tidak menuntut — ia tahu pertanyaan ini tidak butuh dijawab malam ini.
“Belum.” Nisa menyandarkan kepalanya ke bahu Reza. “Tapi aku tidak takut dengan kedua kemungkinannya.”
Reza mengangguk. “Itu cukup.”
“Kamu benar-benar tidak punya preferensi?”
“Preferensiku sudah aku sampaikan.” Ia menoleh, mengecup puncak kepala Nisa pelan. “Apapun yang membuatmu bahagia dan sehat. Itu yang aku mau.”
“Itu bukan jawaban yang membantu.”
“Itu satu-satunya jawaban yang jujur.”
Nisa terdiam sejenak. Lalu tertawa kecil — tawa yang lelah dan bahagia sekaligus, tawa seseorang yang sudah tidak perlu membuktikan apa pun kepada siapa pun termasuk dirinya sendiri.
Di bawah, dari arah kamar tamu paviliun, terdengar suara televisi yang tiba-tiba mati. Lalu suara pintu dibuka setengah, dan suara Alex yang masih setengah mengantuk:
“Papa, Mama — besok sarapan di luar ya? Lex kangen nasi goreng Istana.”
Nisa dan Reza saling pandang.
“Nasi goreng Istana itu bisa dibuat di sini juga, Lex,” Reza menjawab ke arah suara itu.
“Tapi lebih enak kalau makan di teras sama kamu dan Mama.”
Keheningan sebentar.
“Oke,” kata Nisa. “Jam tujuh.”
“Jam delapan.”
“Jam tujuh setengah.”
Bunyi pintu tertutup. Lalu senyap.
Reza menatap Nisa. Nisa menatap Reza.
Tawa mereka pecah bersamaan — pelan, tidak ingin membangunkan Alex yang pasti sudah tertidur kembali dalam dua puluh detik, tapi nyata dan lepas dan sangat milik mereka berdua.
Melodi yang Reza buat mengalir terus dari pemutar musik yang kecil.
Di langit Jakarta yang malam ini memutuskan untuk ramah, satu atau dua bintang terlihat di antara cahaya kota yang tidak pernah benar-benar mati.
Dua puluh tiga tahun.
Bukan dua puluh tiga tahun tanpa luka. Bukan tanpa malam-malam di mana segalanya terasa terlalu berat. Bukan tanpa retakan yang sempat terasa seperti tidak bisa ditambal.
Tapi dua puluh tiga tahun yang dipilih — setiap harinya, setiap paginya, setiap momen kecil di mana keduanya bisa memilih untuk tidak lagi melanjutkan tapi memilih untuk tetap ada.
Kintsugi.

Keindahan dari bekas retakan yang ditambal bukan dengan cara menyembunyikannya, tapi dengan cara merayakannya — mengakui bahwa ini pernah retak, ini pernah hampir hancur, dan justru itulah yang membuatnya kuat.
Di bawah sana, Indonesia terus bergerak.
Rahmawati sedang menutup kantornya untuk malam ini, menyiapkan jadwal klien untuk besok.
Hendri sedang makan malam bersama putrinya yang sudah semester enam.
Pak Darmawan sedang membalas email seorang mantan murid yang mengabarkan ia baru saja menikah — usia dua puluh empat tahun, sudah bekerja, sudah punya tabungan, sudah siap.

Dan di ribuan rumah lain yang tersebar di seluruh kepulauan ini — ada percakapan-percakapan kecil yang terjadi. Tentang ekspektasi. Tentang kesiapan. Tentang hak untuk berkata tidak atau berkata belum atau berkata: aku mau tapi dengan cara yang benar.
Percakapan yang empat tahun lalu tidak punya landasan hukum. Sekarang punya.
Benih yang ditanam — tumbuh.
Tidak sempurna. Tidak seragam. Tidak sesuai rencana di setiap sudutnya.
Tapi tumbuh.
“Za.”
“Hm?”
Nisa tidak menoleh dari langit yang sedang ia tatap. “Makasih sudah mau bersamaku sejauh ini.”
Reza menggenggam tangannya lebih erat.
“Sejauh ini dan seterusnya,” katanya.
Melodi mengalir.
Cahaya kota berkilauan.

Dan di balkon kecil yang sudah menjadi saksi bisu terlalu banyak hal penting — dua orang yang memilih satu sama lain, hari ini dan setiap hari sebelumnya, berdiri berdampingan dalam keheningan yang paling hangat yang bisa ada.
Tidak ada badai yang selamanya.
Tapi ada cahaya yang tidak perlu badai untuk ada.
Cahaya itu ada di sini.
Selalu sudah ada.
— TAMAT —
— Selesai, Epilog —

1: Istana Negara, Jakarta
October 30, 2044, 10:05 AM

Camera flashes struck without pause, rattling like a string of silver fireworks bouncing off the cold marble walls of the Credential Room at Istana Negara. That morning, the room that usually bore silent witness to ambassadors presenting their letters of credence had been transformed into a bustling impromptu press conference. The air felt thick with a mix of expensive perfume, the sweat of news hunters, and a trembling anticipation. Dozens of journalists — from major established outlets to online news portals barely a year old — crowded in an unruly formation behind the thin, deep-red cordon. Microphones jutted forward from every direction, like a pack of hungry metal snakes fighting over prey, all aimed at the two figures sitting calmly at the head table.
They were the room's center of gravity. The nation's epicenter of attention.
The tenth President of the Republic of Indonesia, Nisa Shabrina Farha, and her soulmate, Reza Satria.

Today was not just another day amid the capital's political whirlwind that never truly stopped spinning. Today marked nineteen years of their marriage — a milestone that felt rare, nearly impossible, for a couple living under the microscopic spotlight of the highest office. Especially for the two of them, a couple whose dynamic often made protocol officials frown deeply, yet was loved by millions of citizens for its unfaked honesty and warmth. Nineteen years sailing the ship of marriage through recurring political storms, relentless public pressure, and the immense weight of state responsibility — that was no small feat. It was a miracle tended to every single day.

Nisa looked as she always did: elegant with a simplicity that felt natural, not forced. She wore a modern batik tunic in soft blue, its cut flowing along her slender figure, its long sleeves hanging neatly. For the bottom, she chose ivory-white long trousers that gave off both a professional and feminine impression — two things she always managed to blend without seeming to try hard. Her pale blue hijab was styled in a simple yet elegant modern way, framing her well-kept, light-brown-skinned face. A small, gleaming pearl brooch was pinned neatly at the side of her hijab, the only accessory she wore today.

Her warm smile had already bloomed before she even sat down — Nisa's signature smile that always seemed ready to burst into a light laugh at any moment, contagious and disarming of tension wherever she went. But anyone who knew her well would catch something behind that cheerfulness: a thin trace of fatigue in her sharp eyes, the residue of a marathon meeting that had run until dawn about a budget deficit projection worsening faster than expected. She sat upright, radiating a leader's confidence, yet with an open posture that invited closeness rather than distance.

Beside her, Reza was the embodiment of a calm that soothed and always held a surprise in reserve. In a long-sleeved batik shirt with a parang motif matching the color of Nisa's tunic — a small detail that surely didn't escape the sharp eyes of fashion journalists — he radiated a solid, supportive presence, like a rock choosing to stand right beside a lighthouse rather than in front of it. His black hair, now dusted with silver at both temples, only added to his charisma, lending depth to a face that still carried the playful smile of a man who had never really felt old. His hand moved lightly now and then, touching the back of Nisa's chair — a small, almost invisible gesture, but to anyone who understood their body language, it was Reza's way of saying: I'm here. I'm always here.

The photo session ran for the first few minutes, camera lenses competing to capture the best moment. Then the protocol chief gave a signal, and the room gradually quieted — a fragile quiet, full of held-back anticipation.

The first journalist to raise his hand was a young man from an entertainment news portal, his face still flushed red with excitement, standing in the very front row exactly as he had planned since dawn.

"Ma'am, Nisa! Sir, Reza!" he called out, his voice slightly shrill cutting through the newly formed silence. "How does it feel, your 19th anniversary with Pak Reza this year? Nineteen years, ma'am, sir!"
He paused. One second. Two seconds.

Perhaps his editorial brain had just fired an alarm, because his face suddenly changed color — from excited pink to embarrassed tomato-red — and he hastily corrected himself with very visible panic. "I mean... does it feel good and delicious, ma'am? Eh, no! I mean... solemn, ma'am? Yes, solemn?"
The correction, which only dug the hole deeper, drew a small laugh from several colleagues behind him. Someone could even be heard failing rather badly to hold back a snicker.
Nisa couldn't hold it in.

Her free, contagious laugh — the exact same laugh often quoted by the media as "President Nisa's secret diplomatic weapon" — instantly filled every corner of the room, bouncing off the marble pillars and the thick maroon carpet. That laugh seemed to grant everyone official permission to relax a little, to drop the mental script they had memorized since the night before.

"Yes, thank God, sir," Nisa answered, her eyes glinting playfully at the young journalist who now looked as if he wanted to melt into a puddle on the floor. She deliberately used the casual term of address, making it feel like an ordinary chat rather than a state interview. "Good and solemn, hehehe." She deliberately repeated both word choices, raising an eyebrow slightly in a teasing way. "There, no need to erase it, no need to sweep away your first sentence just now."
The whole room burst into laughter at once — including several photographers who should have been focused on their lenses.

"Honestly, it's fine to be honest in front of me," Nisa continued, her tone light but carrying genuine warmth. Laughter rippled again. The journalists seemed to get a green light to step a little out of the formal questions they had neatly typed into their notepads. "Of course it feels good," she added confidently, glancing briefly at Reza beside her. "After all, Pak Reza here is my husband, whom I love most..."

"Excuse me, ma'am?" A middle-aged female journalist from a well-known women's magazine pounced quickly from the left row, perhaps having been waiting for that opening the whole time. Her tone mixed curiosity with the subtle provocation that had become her trademark over twenty years of career. "Does Ma'am have another husband besides Pak Reza? Why say 'my husband, whom I love most'? There's emphasis on the word 'most,' ma'am."
Nisa shook her head slowly, her smile still perfectly in place, not the least bit provoked. There was a small relief on her face suggesting she was actually enjoying this moment.

"Oh, no, not at all, miss," she said, her tone made to sound slightly, mock-annoyed — a tried-and-true tactic proven a thousand times over. "Well, that's why when someone's talking, you should listen all the way through, until the comma is clear, before asking, before commenting." She looked gently at the journalist, without a trace of anger. "So we don't get our wires crossed and short-circuited over and over again like just now, hehehe..."
Light laughter filled the room again. The journalist smiled a little embarrassed, but actually looked more relaxed than before.
Reza beside her chuckled softly, his gaze at Nisa full of an adoration that had long stopped needing words to be expressed.

"Yes, ma'am, sorry," the young journalist spoke up again, his voice now far calmer, as if he had learned something from the earlier interruption. "If we may ask, what's the secret to lasting so long, ma'am, sir? All the way to nineteen years of marriage, especially amid such an extraordinary schedule as this?"
This was the most anticipated question. The whole room fell silent again, dozens of microphones leaning slightly forward.

Nisa turned to Reza — a small habit she always did before answering questions concerning the two of them, as if silently asking for agreement, acknowledging that this wasn't hers alone to answer. Reza gave a small nod, his smile never fading. A deep understanding flowed strongly between that glance, a wordless communication that only forms after years of knowing and choosing each other every single day.

"Secret?" Nisa tilted her head slightly, her lips pursing in mock deep thought. Several cameras captured the moment. "Actually," she continued, her tone light and flowing again, "there's no secret-keeping at all between us — that's the secret. Total openness. That's what makes it last and stay enjoyable to this day." She paused for a moment, letting her words sink into the air that now felt a little warmer, then turned back to her husband. "Right, sir?"

Before Reza could answer with his usually more poetic philosophy, a more senior male journalist — known around the Palace for questions that sometimes crossed the line but always escaped sanction because the results always went viral — chimed in from the side, half-serious, half-teasing.
"Well... it's probably mostly the, uh, physical relationship that's kept 'hot,' isn't it, ma'am?"
Half a second of silence.
Then Reza burst into laughter.

A deep, unrestrained, thoroughly genuine laugh — the exact same laugh he often let out at home when something was truly hilarious. "Hey, this guy! Wkwkwk!" he exclaimed, looking thoroughly entertained. "Don't bring that up here, sir, I'm embarrassed just saying it." He turned to Nisa, whose cheeks were already flushed pink even though she couldn't hold back her wide smile. This was a moment very much their own — able to turn potential awkwardness into humor within seconds.

"Well, speaking as a man," Reza continued, deciding to go along with the flow of the conversation rather than fight it, his tone playful but with a very familiar mischievous glint in his eyes. "Yes, mainly that, well... so I always stay 'hot,'" he paused dramatically, glancing at Nisa from the corner of his eye, "and passionate." His laughter erupted again, louder this time. "What else could it be? You too, right, ma'am? You also like... that..." He looked at Nisa with a thoroughly teasing gaze, "Hahahahaah!" — deliberately not finishing his sentence, letting the whole room's wild imagination do the rest of the work.

The room was now truly abuzz with laughter. One photographer even lowered his camera for a moment because he couldn't stop laughing. Nisa pinched her husband's arm lightly under the table — an intimate gesture caught by at least three different lenses and destined to become the most-quoted photo the next morning.

"But you don't say that here, sir... Hehehehee..." Nisa replied, half-scolding, half-amused herself. Her cheeks were still flushed, but her eyes shone with a happiness that could only be seen when someone was truly glad to be exactly where they were, with the person they loved.

"Well, what about you, ma'am?" Reza continued, his tone shifting a little more serious, but still warm — he took the chance to slip in something more meaningful amid the laughter. "You said you wanted to be a proper and honest example for every aspect of our lives as a nation, as citizens... Well, that starts from our own family and household life too, doesn't it, ma'am?" He looked at Nisa intently, his gaze now full of meaning beyond the joking. "Who else can we hope will fix and inspire our whole society together, if not starting from us?" He paused briefly, his eyes still playful but something heavier flowing beneath. "Remember, ma'am. You becoming president, the responsibility is for this world and the next, hehehe...." Though ending in a small laugh, there was real weight in those words — weight only felt if you were close enough to hear the tone behind his voice.
Nisa let out a slow breath. Her smile softened into a more private, deeper smile — a smile she kept especially for moments when Reza managed to touch on something true.

"Hm hm hm... there he goes again," she murmured softly, more to herself, but her eyes shone in agreement. She turned back to face the crowd of journalists, straightening her posture slightly. "Well, basically," she summed up in her straightforward, down-to-earth way, "keeping intimacy of body and soul, keeping communication open, keeping the affection and the sparks of love alive... so the fire doesn't go out." She winked with a teasing style that was uniquely Nisa. "Hehehehee... alright? That's enough of an answer, right? We're going to head off now, going to continue celebrating."
"Where are you headed, ma'am? Sir?" someone asked quickly from the right corner, not wanting to miss the last chance.

"Wouldn't you like to know!" Nisa answered quickly in a joking tone, then laughed again — a short but genuine laugh. "Well, celebrating love, of course. Celebrating these colorful nineteen years. Right, sir?"

"Of course, as if we're going to celebrate inflation reports," Reza replied as he rose to his feet together with Nisa, his arm extending to offer itself to his wife with a motion so automatic, so habitual, it felt like part of his breathing. "Hehehehee..."

Nisa rested her hand on Reza's elbow. They walked side by side leaving the podium, followed by Nisa's final wave to the crowd still abuzz with whispers and the sound of typing keyboards. The journalists were busy summarizing, debating the best news angle, some already typing headlines on their laptops with unconcealed enthusiasm. They had all gotten more than they had hoped for this morning — a portrait of a couple brave enough to be honest, able to laugh about things most people kept tightly hidden, who looked so solid and so in love even under a hundred pairs of foreign eyes.
The great door of the Credential Room closed behind them.

The silence of Istana Negara's long corridor, lit by dim crystal lamps, welcomed them like a different world. The sound of their footsteps met softly on the thick carpet, the only sound besides the gentle hum of the air conditioning flowing behind the tall, varnished walls.
And there, within seconds of the door closing, their public facade fully dissolved.

Reza immediately took Nisa's hand — not looping her arm as in front of the cameras, but holding her fingers in a far more personal way, his fingers interlacing with Nisa's fingers perfectly, as if made to fill exactly the gaps that existed. Nisa didn't ask for it. She didn't need to. This had already happened thousands of times, in thousands of different corridors, over the past nineteen years.

"You were really something just now," Nisa whispered as she nudged her husband's waist lightly, the corner of her mouth unable to hold back an amused smile even as she tried. "Talking about 'hot' and everything in front of the journalists."

Reza laughed — a laugh different from before, deeper, more private, more theirs alone. He pulled Nisa a little closer to his side as they walked, his arm looping lightly around her waist. "Let them... let them know too that the president has a normal, happy husband, hahahaa!" he replied playfully, his eyes gleaming as he looked at Nisa from the side.
"Normal," Nisa repeated in a flat tone full of amusement. "A normal husband."
"Very normal."
"Za."
"Very, very normal."
Nisa elbowed him again, harder this time, and Reza laughed heartily in the empty corridor, not caring about the echo it caused.

They walked slower than they needed to, savoring this rare silence — a silence that demanded nothing of them, that recorded nothing, analyzed nothing, judged nothing. This was where they were most themselves: two people who happened to also lead a nation, but now were simply walking together down a dimly lit corridor, hand in hand, laughing about small things.

Their footsteps met softly on the thick carpet, the only sound accompanying that afternoon. The weight of the state briefly evaporated — replaced by the warm anticipation of the evening they had planned since a week ago. An evening that belonged only to them. An evening with no agenda, no schedule, no cameras.

At one corner of the corridor, a young presidential guard stood at attention, gaze fixed straight ahead, trying hard to be a wall that neither saw nor heard. The corner of his mouth might have lifted slightly, but he managed to hold it back.
Managed, barely, though.
Nisa glanced at the guard briefly, then whispered to Reza: "Poor Mas Anto."
"Why?" Reza whispered back.
"Having to pretend not to hear your laugh just now."
Reza glanced toward Mas Anto, then back at Nisa, and both of them held back their laughter in a way that made their shoulders shake together in silence.
Nineteen years.
And still like this.

Meanwhile, on another side of the same city, another story was waiting to be found — a story that would change everything, starting from a small piece of news tucked in the corner of an online portal's page that no one at the Palace could imagine would set the country ablaze.
But that was for later.
For now, there was a hand holding a hand. There was laughter echoing down a long corridor. There were nineteen years that felt like a beginning, not an end.
And that was already more than enough.
— End of Chapter 1 —

2: The President's Private Pavilion, Istana Negara
October 30, 2044, Evening
The sun had long given up on Jakarta's horizon.

All that remained were dramatic streaks of orange and purple fading slowly in the western sky, like a painter erasing their own work before darkness took over completely. City lights began to glimmer one by one, like jewels scattered across a deepening black velvet.

Far from the noise and formality of Istana Negara, tucked among a lush, well-tended garden — tropical trees whose canopies intertwined naturally, the faint scent of jasmine drifting through the night air — Nisa and Reza's private pavilion stood as a fortress of calm. A sanctuary. The place where those two words — president and first gentleman — were left at the door like a pair of wet shoes not allowed inside.
This was where they became simply themselves.
Nisa and Reza.

Inside the warm family room, the atmosphere felt like an entirely different world from that morning's commotion. Light from a few sandalwood-and-lavender aromatherapy candles danced on the walls, small shadows swaying gently with the barely-there airflow from the vents. The two scents blended into something more than fragrance — something that felt like home, like a long breath after running a great distance.
From a corner of the room, Reza's beloved record player spun a classic instrumental — Miles Davis, Kind of Blue — soft and floating, filling the gaps of silence without forcing itself.
Their batik outfits were long since changed.

Nisa wore ivory silk pajamas that fell softly along her figure, while Reza had on a midnight-blue cotton shirt and thin trousers he had washed so many times the fabric had gone perfectly soft. They sat close together on the plush, deep emerald velvet sofa — a sofa that had silently witnessed far too many important conversations, laughs, small arguments that ended with a kiss on the forehead, and of course, private moments they never told anyone about.

The exhaustion of the whole day — the smile that had to stay fixed in place, the diplomatic answers that had to be carefully worded, the dozens of cameras watching every expression — all of it simply dissolved here. Like taking off a heavy suit of armor after a long battle.

Nisa rested her head on Reza's shoulder, her jet-black hair falling loose, framing a face that looked softer without its official makeup. Her sharp eyes, usually full of strategic calculation, had softened now, glinting in the dim candlelight. There was a vulnerability there that only appeared here, only for Reza — a part of herself she never showed on any podium, that no camera had ever caught.

Reza gently stroked the curve of her waist through the silk of her pajamas — a touch so familiar Nisa didn't need to look to know exactly what it felt like. Calming. Like electricity that didn't sting, only flowed.
“Tired?” Reza asked softly, his voice deep and low, meant only for Nisa's ears.
“A bit.” Nisa let out a long breath. “But the good kind of tired.”
She lifted her head slightly, glancing at Reza from the corner of her eye. “You were really something this morning, Za. In front of all those journalists.”
“Something how?”
“That 'hot' thing.”
Reza chuckled quietly — a laugh different from his public one, darker and warmer at once. “Well, it's true.”
“Not embarrassed?”
“Embarrassed in front of who?” He glanced at Nisa with an expression too relaxed to be accidental. “In front of journalists who have the same biological needs?”
Nisa pinched his arm.

Reza laughed again, more freely this time, the sound echoing softly through the warm room, mixing with the floating Miles Davis. Nisa couldn't help smiling along, though she tried to keep a straight face for a full three seconds before finally giving up.
“Nineteen years,” she murmured quietly once their laughter settled, more to herself. “It doesn't feel real.”

Reza turned, looking at her in the dim light. There was something in his gaze that always made Nisa feel truly seen — not just looked at physically, but genuinely seen, understood down to the parts she never put into words.
“It feels real,” Reza answered quietly. “But it doesn't feel heavy.”
Nisa looked at him for a moment. Then smiled — a small smile that existed nowhere else but here.
What followed was a quiet, private evening between them, the kind of closeness nineteen years of marriage makes room for — one they kept just for themselves, away from any camera or headline.
Afterward, they lay together on the thick carpet in front of the sofa, too content and too lazy to move to the bed only a few steps away. Their breathing slowly settled back into its ordinary rhythm.
A deeply comfortable silence wrapped around the room.

Only their heartbeats gradually slowing. Only the soft rustle of a thin blanket Reza had pulled from somewhere to cover them both. Only Miles Davis still playing from the corner of the room, as if it understood that this moment only needed music, not words.
“Oh my goodness.”
Nisa's voice broke the silence — a hoarse whisper that sounded like someone who had just landed back on earth after a very long journey.
“That was really nice, love. Masyaallah…”
Her head rested on Reza's broad chest, feeling her husband's breathing settle into its steady rhythm, listening to his heartbeat still a little quick.

Reza kissed the top of her head, breathing in the scent of Nisa's hair that always smelled like nothing he could describe except Nisa. “Yeah, it really was, love,” he replied, his voice deep and full of contentment. “Really was.” There was genuine gratitude in it — not just about tonight, but about all of it. Everything they had built together.
Nisa chuckled softly — a satisfied little laugh she never let out in public, one that only comes from truly safe intimacy.

“Hey, hey, hey, love…” Suddenly she lifted her head a little, looking up at Reza's face in the dim light. Something lit up in her eyes, not desire this time, but something else — a different kind of enthusiasm, as if the analytical part of her brain had just switched back on without her permission.
“It's funny, you know.”
Reza furrowed his brow. “Funny what?”
“I just had this little flash of insight.”

Reza's laughter burst out — not a small chuckle, but a real laugh that shook his chest and, with it, Nisa's head resting there. “Hahahahaah… a flash of insight?” His eyes sparkled at his wife with an expression somewhere between amused and impressed. “You and your ideas. What kind of insight now, after all that just now?”

“Oh my gosh, I'm serious!” Nisa gave his chest a small pinch. Reza held back a little wince, ticklish. “You know…” — she paused, her tone suddenly turning sincere without warning — “how dry and empty my life would be without you beside me, Za…”
She kissed his still slightly damp forehead gently.

Reza went quiet for a moment, letting the compliment settle in. Something in his face softened each time Nisa did this — rare moments when she dropped her usual humor and simply received, without deflecting into a joke.
But only for a moment.
“Hmm… this is dangerous, all this praising,” he teased, his eyes lighting up again. “Makes me want to go again. Shall we?” His eyebrows rose with an expression too innocent to be believed.
“Et, et, et — hold on, Mr. President of My Heart,” Nisa tapped his chest lightly, holding back a laugh. “I'm being serious about this insight! Don't you want to know?”
Reza gave in, in a way that showed he genuinely was curious. “Alright, really? What insight? Go on, tell me.”

“Okay, so.” Nisa leaned into his side, her eyes shining with an enthusiasm that reminded Reza of a much younger Nisa, the one he'd first met at a campus discussion forum twenty years ago, the one who always had a theory about everything. “Allah is All-Beautiful, All-Creative, right? But also full of humor, in His own way — He gave us bodies with all these funny, quirky little details.”
Reza nodded slowly, following along.

What followed was some warm, playful teasing between them about the funny little quirks of their own bodies — the kind of easy, unguarded joking that only happens between two people who have shared everything, including their most private moments, for almost two decades.
Reza burst out laughing.

A deep, unrestrained laugh, truly impossible to hold back — the laugh of a man who, after nineteen years with the same person, could still be caught completely off guard. “Oh my goodness, love! How do you even come up with these things!” He answered by tapping her nose.

“Oh, right!! Who said you only had a few funny parts,” Nisa wasn't going to lose this round, her voice already climbing into a high, amused pitch. “Look — everything else is funny too! Your hands are funny, your feet are funny, your ears are funny!”
“You too!” Reza poked her cheek back. “Your eyes are funny, your lips are funny, everything's funny!”
Their laughter filled the quiet room — free, unburdened laughter, pure laughter born of total intimacy and unconditional acceptance. Not laughter for an audience. Not laughter measured or controlled.
Just laughter.

Here, in this room, Nisa wasn't the respected and sometimes feared President of the Republic of Indonesia. Reza wasn't the charismatic First Gentleman who always appeared neatly beside his powerful wife. They were simply Nisa and Reza — two people who loved each other, flaws and all, who found small miracles even in the silliest little things, even after nearly two decades together.
This was their foundation. Laughter. Acceptance. And honesty with no agenda.
The night grew later.

The air began to feel cooler, seeping in from the slightly open window. The aromatherapy candles were running low, their flames shrinking and flickering more often. Miles Davis had long since stopped; the record player spun quietly in the comfortable silence.

In a motion that felt more like a dance than an effort, Reza lifted Nisa from the floor — bridal style, one arm firmly beneath her knees, the other supporting her back — and carried her the few steps to their bed.
Nisa wrapped her arms around his neck, too tired and too content to pretend to protest. “You don't have to—”
“Nineteenth anniversary,” Reza cut in flatly, walking steadily. “I have to.”
Nisa giggled softly against his shoulder.

Under the thick blanket, they settled together again — not with desire this time, only pleasant exhaustion and familiar warmth. Nisa nestled into his side the way muscle memory knew by heart, her head in the curve of his shoulder, one hand on his chest. Reza wrapped an arm around her back, his chin resting on the top of her head.
Their breathing slowed, falling into rhythm together.

Outside, beyond the pavilion's thick walls and the Palace's tall fences, Jakarta kept moving as it always did — traffic still busy, streetlights still blinking, and somewhere in a corner of the city no one in this room knew about, a small piece of news was waiting to be found.
News that would change everything.
But that was for later.
For now, there was warmth beneath a thick blanket. There was breathing in the same rhythm. There were nineteen years that felt like a foundation, not a burden.
And there was Reza whispering quietly — so quietly, almost inaudible, perhaps not even sure himself if Nisa was already asleep:
“Thank you for being my wife, Sa.”
Silence. Then:
“Thank you for being my husband, Za.”
Both fell asleep with a smile that no one could see except the bedroom ceiling and one small candle in the corner of the room, which finally went out too, leaving behind a perfect, peaceful darkness.
— End of Chapter 2 —
