3: The President's Office, Istana Negara
October 30, 2044, 4:30 PM

Golden afternoon sunlight cut through the tall windows on the west side of the President's Office, casting long shadows over stacks of documents and a few award plaques arranged on a bookshelf. In a corner of the room, the small coffee machine had just finished brewing Gayo coffee — its aroma drifting faintly, mixing with the familiar smell of paper and the cool air from the AC.

Unlike the grand, formal Credential Room that morning, this room felt more personal. This was Nisa's true space — efficient, modern, focused on function, yet holding warmth in its corners. There was no intimidating mahogany desk. Instead, there was a standing desk near the window and a teal velvet sofa that had already borne the weight of hundreds of important decisions and a few tears no one ever knew about.

A few family photos in simple silver frames decorated the corner of the desk — their wedding photo from nineteen years ago with awkward smiles that still amused Nisa every time she saw it, a photo from their last family trip with Alex to Raja Ampat the year before, and one candid shot Reza had taken in secret: Nisa asleep on the sofa with a policy document still in her hand, Alex sitting on the floor near her feet doing homework.
That photo had never been shared anywhere.

Nisa had just finished her last meeting of the day — a tense video conference discussion with the Minister of Public Works about accelerating connectivity infrastructure in eastern Indonesia. The virtual ministers had logged off a few minutes ago. Now she was alone in the vast room.
She took off her reading glasses, rubbing the bridge of her nose gently, feeling the strain there.

Tired. The familiar kind of tired — the kind that wouldn't disappear with sleep alone, the kind that came from hours of managing expectations, holding compromises together, and making sure every gear of government kept turning in the same direction without anything slipping loose along the way.
On a whim, she picked up her personal tablet and opened one of the online news portals.

The top headlines were still dominated by echoes of that morning's interview. "19 Years of Nisa-Reza: Candidly Revealing the Secret to Their Harmony," "Reza Satria's Blunt Style Steals the Spotlight Again," "President Nisa: Never Assume You Know Your Partner Completely." In the comments section, netizens flooded it with praise. #CoupleGoals. The couple everyone dreams of. An inspiration to the nation.
A small, tired smile crossed Nisa's lips.
Then her finger kept scrolling down — and stopped.
Her eyes fixed on a headline placed far below all the articles of celebration and praise. The words felt like a slap to the face:
“****Tragic: Young Woman in Sukamaju Village Ends Her Life, Allegedly Due to Forced Marriage to Man Chosen by Her Parents.****”
Nisa clicked the link.
The story unfolded slowly.

An eighteen-year-old girl. Recently graduated high school with excellent grades — ranked third in her school, with a simple dream of studying education and becoming an elementary school teacher. Not an extravagant dream. The same dream shared by millions of other girls across the far corners of the country.
That dream fell apart.

Her family forced her to marry a man nearly twice her age — a locally wealthy businessman known to be harsh, whose first marriage had ended in divorce. The reason: the family's tight finances, and the pressure to "protect the family's good name" because the man had proposed with a dowry too large to refuse.
The girl's protests were ignored. Her tears dismissed as nothing. People around her said: "That's just how it is, she'll accept it eventually."

A few months after the marriage she never wanted, she was found dead, having hanged herself in a room that had once been full of band posters and schoolbooks. She left one last letter — not a letter full of anger, but one full of questions more painful than anger: Why did my dreams have to be taken from me? What did I do wrong wanting to study? Why does marriage have to be like this?
Nisa set down her tablet.
Her hands felt cold.
She rose from her chair and walked slowly toward the window, looking down at the Palace garden below, lit by the same golden afternoon light that had illuminated their celebration that morning.
The irony hit her with a force she hadn't anticipated.

That morning, she and Reza had sat in the Credential Room, surrounded by camera flashes and journalists fighting over microphones, answering questions about the secret to a lasting, harmonious marriage. The public celebrated them. Comments online were filled with hearts and stars. #CoupleGoals. A couple proving that love could survive even under the pressure of the highest power in the land.

And on that very same day, in another corner of this country, an eighteen-year-old girl closed her eyes forever because of that very same institution. Marriage. Something that was supposed to be a harbor for love — had instead become a prison.
Something that was supposed to give hope — had instead taken away the only thing she had.
Nisa gripped the edge of the window.
And suddenly, unbidden, a memory she had long kept locked away came flooding back — a memory she had never fully told anyone, not even Reza.

Years ago, at the darkest peak of her family's rejection of her relationship with Reza, her father Ahmed had once, in one moment of furious despair, threatened to arrange her marriage to the son of an old business colleague — a young man Nisa had never really known, whom she had only met once at a family event years before. "Instead of insisting on that infidel DJ," her father had said then, his voice cold and cutting in a way she had never heard before, "it's better if Papa finds you a match whose religion is clear, whose family is clear. You're old enough. It's time." For days afterward, the house that used to be her refuge turned into a space of silent pressure — closed-door conversations between Ahmed and the colleague's family that she could faintly hear through her bedroom door, hopeful looks from her mother wishing her daughter would "come to her senses" and accept the safer path.

Nisa was never actually forced all the way to the altar — with a courage that nearly exhausted every last bit of resolve she had at the time, she managed to hold her ground, refusing firmly even though it cost her weeks of a frozen household atmosphere. But the fear from that time — the fear that her life, her body, her future could simply be decided by someone else in the name of "good" and "propriety," without ever truly being asked what she wanted — never fully went away. She had only buried that fear, the same way she had buried her dream of becoming president, deep beneath the calmer layers of life she later built with Reza.
She survived. She was fortunate. She married for love, by her own conscious choice, to someone who respected her as a whole person, not as a family asset to be "secured" through the right marriage.

But the girl in Sukamaju hadn't been as fortunate as her. And Nisa knew that somewhere in this country, at this very moment, there were thousands of other women living through a crueler version of what had nearly happened to her — without a Reza to fight for, without the courage she had somehow found back then, without luck on their side.

This isn't the first time, something whispered in her head. This isn't an isolated case. This is a symptom. A disease that had been left to fester for too long beneath a surface that still looked fine.

Numbers she had long since memorized from various reports began spinning through her mind — no longer as abstract data, but as real faces. Millions of girls whose dreams were buried under the weight of tradition and economic pressure. Thousands of domestic violence cases that were only the tip of an iceberg of silent suffering behind tightly closed doors. A young generation entering marriage not by conscious choice, but because no other choice was allowed.
And the state, all this time, had chosen to stay silent.
Calling it "a private matter." "A family affair." "Not something to interfere with."
Not anymore, Nisa hissed inwardly. Her resolve hardened like freshly tempered steel.
Never again.

She returned to her desk with a different stride than ten minutes before. The exhaustion was still there, but now something burned beneath it — an ember she had long known was there, but today had caught a wind that meant it could no longer simply smolder in silence.

With quick, decisive movements, she opened the notes app on her work laptop. Her slender fingers began moving across the keyboard, pouring out ideas that had been circling in her head for months — ideas she had held back because she knew how great the political risk was, how fierce the resistance would be, how unpopular a move like this would be in the short term.
But there was an eighteen-year-old girl who could no longer wait for policies that were popular.
INITIAL DRAFT — POLICY FRAMEWORK:
National Marriage Readiness Standard: must be clear, measurable. Focus on mental maturity and basic financial independence readiness — not just biological age.

Comprehensive and MANDATORY Pre-Marital Education: not a two-hour formality. Material: legal rights and obligations, reproductive health, conflict management, family finances, basic parenting. Must be relevant and modern.
Mandatory Pre-Marital Counseling: an integral part of the process, not optional. Standardized mental-emotional readiness assessment by professionals.
STRICT Legal Sanctions: for practices of forced marriage or arranged marriage without consent — whether by family, guardians, or anyone else — especially against underage women.
Strengthened Victim Protection: easy access to legal aid, safe houses, and state-supported legal processes in cases of domestic violence or forced marriage.
At the very top of the document, Nisa typed a title firmly:
FAMILY READINESS BILL — Initial Draft.
She stared at those words on her laptop screen for a few seconds.

Outside the window, Jakarta's sky began to change color — darkening orange turning to purple, purple slowly being swallowed by night. City lights began switching on one by one in the distance, like stars descending to earth.
A cup of Gayo coffee beside her had long gone cold. She didn't care.
Her office door opened without a knock first.
A way of entering used by only two people in the entire Palace — Reza, and Alex.
“Oh, Mom's still here?” The voice was flat, casual, but carrying an undisguised note of surprise.

Alex — a slightly faded indie rock band shirt, jeans worn at the knees, limited-edition sneakers Nisa still didn't know the price of because she was afraid to find out — walked in biting into a red apple. Alex scanned the room with the look of someone deciding whether the situation was worth commenting on.
Nisa glanced over. “Where were you?”

“Library.” Alex flopped onto the teal sofa in a way only a teenager who had never experienced back pain could manage. “Working on a history essay. About Soekarno.” Another bite of the apple. “Why does Mom look like she just read bad news?”
“Because I just read bad news.”
“Which one?”
Nisa turned her laptop slightly toward him. Alex leaned forward from the sofa to look — then sat back. The expression shifted, losing the usual layer of irony.
“The girl in Sukamaju,” Alex murmured. Not a question.
Nisa looked over. “You already read it?”
“It was trending on everyone's feed this afternoon.” Alex paused, turning the apple in one hand. “Didn't think Mom read that kind of portal too.”
“Mom reads everything.”
“Bad habit.”
Nisa almost smiled. “Lex.”
“Yeah?”
“Mom's going to draft a bill.”

A brief silence. Alex looked at his mother — not the bored look of a teenager, but a look far older than his years, the kind that occasionally reminded Nisa that their son could no longer be treated as a child needing protection from the world's complexities.
“What bill?”
“Family Readiness.” Nisa pointed to her laptop screen. “Minimum standards before marriage. Mandatory education. Sanctions for those who force it. Real protection for victims.”
Alex nodded slowly, still looking at the screen from a distance. Then he leaned his head back against the sofa and looked up at the ceiling.
“Good idea, Mom.” His voice was flat, but Nisa knew Alex well enough by now to know that flat, here, meant serious. “Revolutionary, even.” A pause. “But yeah, be ready.”
“Ready for what?”

“Getting attacked from every direction.” Alex turned his head to look at Nisa with the expression of an analyst who happened to be fifteen years old. “The 'guardians of national morality' crowd, the 'anti family-liberalization' groups, or whatever cool name they'll come up with. Plus the opposition that's been waiting for an opening from you.” Another bite of the apple. “The Palace is going to be as busy as a night market.”
Nisa looked at her son for a long moment.
“You know that, and you still say the idea is good.”
“Yeah.”
“So you agree with it?”

Alex stood up from the sofa, straightening his shirt without much success. “That means Mom has to do it. If no one's willing to do the right thing out of fear of being attacked, then the wrong side just keeps winning.” He walked toward the door. “That's what Mom always tells me when I'm scared to say something true in front of my friends.”
He paused at the doorway, turning back briefly.
“Don't forget dinner, Mom. Dad already asked what you want to eat.”
The door closed behind him.
Nisa looked at the closed door for a few seconds.
Then she turned back to her laptop screen. To the four words still glowing at the top of the document.
FAMILY READINESS BILL — Initial Draft.

Outside the window, Jakarta was now fully night. City lights glimmered like jewels scattered across the dark. Somewhere out there, in thousands of homes spread across this archipelago, there were women today once again swallowing a bitterness they never chose. There were girls whose dreams were being negotiated away by people claiming to love them. There was a cycle that kept turning because no one dared to jam a wedge into its gears.
Until now, Nisa thought.

She straightened her posture, pushed the now-cold coffee cup to the edge of the desk, and began typing again — faster this time, more certain, like someone who had waited far too long for permission from herself and had finally decided: that permission never needed to be waited for.
She was already far too late.
Now, she was beginning.
The President's Private Bedroom, 10:30 PM

When Reza came into the room with his hair still slightly damp from his shower, he found Nisa already in bed — but not asleep. A book lay open on her lap, but her eyes weren't reading. Her gaze was fixed on a point that existed on none of the bedroom walls.

Reza didn't ask. He walked slowly to the side of the bed, sat on the edge, and with a motion that had become muscle memory over nineteen years, reached for Nisa's feet folded over the blanket, lifted them slightly, and began massaging her soles with just the right pressure.
Nisa closed her eyes for a moment.
“Still thinking about it?” Reza asked softly.
“The news. The girl in Sukamaju.”
Reza nodded, not stopping his massage. “I read it too, this morning.”
A brief silence. Outside the window, Jakarta kept humming through the night.

“Mas,” Nisa finally opened her eyes, looking at her husband. There was something in her gaze that Reza knew very well — not a question, not hesitation, but someone who had already made a decision and now just needed to say it out loud to make it real.
“I want to draft a bill.”
Reza stopped massaging.

“Family Readiness,” Nisa continued. “Minimum standards before marriage. Mandatory education. Real sanctions for those who force it. Protection for victims.” She took a breath. “The state has stayed silent about this for far too long, Mas. I can't stay silent anymore either.”

Reza looked at her for a long moment. Something moved across his face — not doubt, but calculation. Someone who loved deeply enough not to simply say yes before truly understanding what that yes meant.
“That's a very brave idea,” he said finally. Quietly, but sincerely. “A very noble purpose.” A pause. “But you know the consequences, right?”
“A political storm.”

“A massive storm, Sa. Bigger than anything we've faced before.” His hand moved again, gently holding her ankle. “Traditionalist groups who'll feel their customs are being trampled. Conservative groups who'll shout that you're fighting religion. Opportunistic politicians who've been waiting for ammunition to use against you.” His eyes met Nisa's directly. “They'll attack you relentlessly, Sa. Not just the policy — you, personally.”
Nisa didn't look away.
“I know.”
“And you still want to do it?”

“I can't not want to, Mas.” Her voice didn't waver. “There's an eighteen-year-old girl who closed her eyes forever today because no one was willing to do this sooner. How many more have to wait until we feel ready enough?”
Reza was quiet.

He looked at his wife's face in the dim bedroom light — a face he knew better than his own, a face that carried a president's exhaustion but tonight also carried something different. Not anger. Not ambition. Something older and harder than both.
Conviction.
He took both of Nisa's hands, holding them firmly between his warm palms.
“We face it together,” he said. Not an offer. A statement. “Like always.”
Nisa's eyes glistened for a moment — just a moment, then cleared again.
“Like always,” she repeated softly.

The silence that then settled over them wasn't an empty silence. It was a full one — full of understanding that needed no words, commitment that needed no formal vow, and a love that had weathered enough storms to know it wouldn't leave just because the next one was already visible on the horizon.
Out there, beyond the walls and tall fences of the Palace, Indonesia slept, unaware of what had just been decided in this bedroom.
The seed had been planted.
Now all that remained was to wait for the storm to come and test it.
— End of Chapter 3 —
PALACE FULL OF EMBERS
4: The President's Office, Istana Negara
November 1, 2044, 9:15 AM
Two days after the anniversary celebration.

The world had already resumed its normal spin — or rather, the speed that was never truly normal for someone with a position like Nisa's. The first agenda had started at 6:30 AM with the morning intelligence briefing. The second followed at 7:45 — a coordination meeting on accelerating the food program. Now, in the brief gap between the third session that had just ended and the Ministry of Social Affairs coordination meeting starting in an hour, Nisa stood at her standing desk by the window.

In front of her, a large tablet displayed the draft proposal she had worked on for the past three nights — back and forth, crossing out, adding, deleting, until her eyes stung and Reza had to knock on her office door twice to remind her it was past midnight.
INDEPENDENT ADULTHOOD HOUSE PROGRAM
Policy Proposal — Draft 3, November 1, 2044

Nisa's fingers moved across the screen again, adding a point she had just thought of in the shower that morning — about a basic financial literacy module that needed to be a mandatory component of the program. Her brow furrowed, her eyes focused, all her attention pulled into those words.

This program was another answer to the same unease — the unease that had exploded after she read the news about the Sukamaju girl two days ago, a story that turned out not to be new, not the first case, and would not be the last if no one did anything. The Family Readiness Bill was the regulatory approach: setting standards, imposing sanctions, forcing the state to be legally present. But Independent Adulthood House was a different approach — more humane, further upstream. Equipping young people before they arrived at that crossroads. An intensive, possibly residential, program for youths aged 17-18. Not a two-hour pre-marital course that was mere formality. This one was real.
Emotional maturity. Basic financial independence. Rights and responsibilities in a household. Comprehensive, taboo-free reproductive health. Conflict management. Psychologically healthy parenting.
A foundation before the building, Nisa thought. Not just patching cracks downstream.
“Ma'am…”

That voice — soft, measured, and a touch too polished for Nisa's taste on a morning already this packed — broke her concentration. Angel Marina stood at the half-open door, her figure perfectly neat in a cream blouse and gray pencil skirt. In her hands, a thick cream-colored folder. Her expression, as usual, was a blend of total professionalism and slight discomfort — the expression of someone bringing news that might not be met with a smile.
Nisa tapped the save icon on her tablet before setting it down. “What is it, Ngel?”

“Your visit schedule to the MSME training center in South Tangerang tomorrow is finalized. Transportation and security have been coordinated.” Angel opened her folder, her eyes dropping to the first page. “And… there are several response memos in, ma'am. From the Directorate General of Islamic Community Guidance, the Ministry of Social Affairs, and BKKBN. All related to the initial draft proposal for Independent Adulthood House.”

The way Angel said several response memos — with a small pause before the word “and,” with a tone that dipped slightly lower at the end of the sentence — was already enough for Nisa to guess the content before opening it.
She let out a long breath. “Don't tell me it's exactly the same as last week, Ngel.”

Angel hesitated slightly. “There are a few technical points raised, ma'am. Mainly related to long-term funding sources, inclusive participant criteria, and… some questions about potential friction with cultural and religious values.”

“Which means,” Nisa cut in, looking straight at Angel, “they're worried this is too unconventional, too bold, and will trigger controversy. And those safe, normative sentences are being used to avoid having to take a clear stance.” She raised an eyebrow. “Right?”
Angel didn't answer, but her expression already had.

Nisa rubbed her temple. “I need concrete input, Ngel. Constructive criticism or clear support. Not just the go-to line 'in principle we support this, but an in-depth study from various aspects is needed.' In-depth study after in-depth study — when do we actually start moving?”

“I understand, ma'am.” Angel opened to the next page. “One more thing. A representative from the Moderate Ulama Forum has sent a request for an audience next week. It seems related to some points you mentioned in your latest statement about marriage readiness.”

Nisa nodded without hesitation. “Schedule it as soon as possible, Ngel. Prepare the materials. I'm always ready for dialogue. It's actually good if someone wants a serious discussion — with arguments and data, not just shouting from behind the scenes with no solutions.”
“Controversy is Mom's middle name.”
Nisa didn't need to turn around to know who had just walked into her office without knocking.

Alex — the same slightly faded indie rock band shirt as yesterday and the day before, jeans worn at the knees, limited-edition sneakers Nisa still had never asked the price of — leaned casually against the now wide-open doorframe. In his hand, a pack of crackers he bit into casually, as if the office of the President of the Republic of Indonesia were a hallway in his school cafeteria.
Angel, who was flipping to the third page of her folder, reflexively straightened her posture and pretended to be deeply interested in that page's contents.

“Besides,” Alex continued, walking in uninvited and dropping onto the teal sofa in a way only someone who'd never experienced chronic back pain could manage, “why bother thinking about marriage so much? Who even needs marriage when you can be happy as a quality single person…” he paused, turning his head toward Angel with a very deliberate grin, “…like Auntie Angel here?”
Angel's face instantly turned as colorful as a rainy-season rainfall map. She turned her face to the left, pretending to be very busy adjusting the folder in her hands for the third time.
“Alexander Damar Satria.”
Nisa's voice wasn't loud. But there was a certain tone in it — a tone Alex had memorized since he was four years old — far more effective than any raise in volume.
Alex raised both hands, a surrender gesture that wasn't really surrender. “Okay, okay. Just stating facts, Mom.”
“Stop teasing Angel. Have some pity.”

“So much pity,” Alex repeated in a tone that didn't sound the least bit apologetic, but he shifted to the edge of the sofa in a way that might have been meant as a gesture of good faith. “But seriously, Mom.” He took another bite of his cracker, and this time his expression changed — the layer of irony he always wore like a jacket slipped down slightly, revealing something underneath that was older and more serious than his age. “The program's good. Revolutionary, even.” A pause. “But yeah, be ready.”
Nisa turned to look at her son. “Ready for what?”

“Getting attacked from every direction. The 'guardians of national morality' crowd, the 'anti family-liberalization' groups, whatever cool name they'll come up with. Plus the opposition that's been waiting for this chance for ages.” He looked at Nisa, directly this time, not from the corner of his eye. “They're going to milk this for everything it's worth.”
Nisa didn't answer right away.

Sometimes — and this was one of those moments — she saw a shadow of someone in Alex's face that made her breath catch for a second. Not Reza, though Alex inherited much from his father. But something deeper than that — the way Alex saw patterns, the way he connected dots that hadn't yet been connected, the way he delivered uncomfortable truths in a tone too flat to be accidental.
An inheritance from me too, maybe, Nisa thought.

“Mom knows, Lex,” she said finally, her tone gentler than before. “That's exactly why, knowing there will be attacks, this voice has to keep existing. A voice reminding everyone that the true essence of religious teaching should liberate, not restrain. Rahmatan lil alamin — mercy for all creation. Not a selective mercy that can be used as a tool to force people into marriage before they're ready.”
Alex nodded slowly. Silent for a moment. Then he got up from the sofa.
“Alright then,” he murmured, walking toward the door with the casual stride that had become his trademark, “get ready for this Palace to get even busier than a night market.”
He disappeared through the door.
Nisa almost smiled despite having nearly been annoyed moments ago.
Angel, who had been heroically holding back any reaction to Alex's presence, finally cleared her throat softly. “Shall I continue summarizing the points from the memos, ma'am?”
“Yes, Ngel. Also prepare—”
“Tired?”
That voice came from the doorway, now open wider — deep, warm, and so familiar that Nisa's shoulders reflexively relaxed half a centimeter before she even realized it.

Reza stood in the doorway. A dark blue long-sleeved shirt, cream chinos, hair that looked like it had just been combed but not too seriously. In his hands, two artisan ceramic mugs — their favorite mugs, bought from a ceramic craftsman in Ubud seven years ago. Thin wisps of steam rose from both, and the accompanying aroma immediately filled the entire room.
Gayo arabica coffee.
Nisa couldn't hold back her smile. Her previously tense face instantly changed — like someone who had been running a long time and suddenly found a chair. “Pa!”
Reza walked in, stopped in front of Nisa, and handed over one mug carefully. “Your favorite Gayo arabica. A little creamer, no sugar.”
Then he leaned down, kissing Nisa's forehead gently.

A brief kiss, no more than two seconds. But in front of Angel, who immediately became very busy staring at a corner of the ceiling with unnatural intensity, that kiss felt like something more than mere affection — it was Reza's way of saying I know your morning has been heavy, I'm here, take a breath for a moment.
Nisa took a deep sip of her coffee.
Just the right heat. The right acidity. A hint of caramel at the finish that she always loved. Her eyes closed for a second, savoring it.
“Thank you so much, Za.” She lowered her mug, looking at her husband. “The timing is perfect. I was getting overwhelmed thinking about bureaucratic memos that say the same thing week after week.”
Reza sat in a chair across from her desk, sipping his coffee. “Which memos?”
“Responses to Independent Adulthood House.” Nisa sat in her chair, turning her tablet screen slightly toward Reza. “From three ministries. Content… well, you can guess yourself.”
“'In principle we support it, but an in-depth study is needed'?”
Nisa laughed lightly, tired but genuine. “Exactly.”

Reza nodded slowly, his face serious. “I figured. But your idea is excellent, Sa. Really important. Don't let those dissonant voices make you doubt yourself.” His eyes looked at Nisa directly, a look he never used for small talk. “Besides,” he added, a thin smile appearing at the corner of his mouth, “aren't you at your most radiant when you're making conservatives lose their minds?”
Nisa elbowed him. “Oh please. But yeah, kind of.”

“But seriously, Sa.” Reza's tone shifted slightly, heavier. He set his mug on the desk. “I've heard from a few colleagues — the opposition groups are really consolidating now. Not just about this program, but the whole direction of your policies touching social and cultural issues. They'll look for openings. Any size.” He took Nisa's hand on the desk, holding it. “Be careful, okay?”
Nisa nodded. Reza's grip felt the way it always did — like an anchor. “I know. But I'm not backing down, Za.”

“I know you won't.” Reza smiled — not a worried smile, but the smile of someone who had known his wife long enough to know that not backing down wasn't just words. “That's why I'm here.” He tightened his grip. “We're a team. One package. Remember?”
“I remember.”

Angel, who had been standing very straight in the corner of the room with the expression of a professional deeply respecting her boss's privacy, cleared her throat softly for the second time. “Ma'am, sorry — there's one more agenda item to confirm. The Ministry of Social Affairs coordination meeting starts in fifty minutes, and you still need to read the summary—”

“Yes, Ngel, one moment.” Nisa reluctantly released Reza's hand, straightened her shoulders, and returned to the mode her entire staff knew well — focused, efficient, in motion. “Please schedule the Moderate Ulama Forum audience as soon as possible. Also prepare a summary of all the crucial points from those memos. We'll discuss the response strategy after lunch.”
“Yes, ma'am.” Angel immediately began typing notes on her tablet.
Reza rose from his chair, taking his nearly finished coffee mug. He walked toward the door, then stopped, turning to Nisa.

“Don't skip lunch again, okay.” His tone was light, but Nisa knew it wasn't just a casual suggestion — yesterday she'd skipped lunch because of an unplanned emergency meeting, and Reza had been quietly annoyed about it since the afternoon.
“I promise.”
“A promise that's enforceable?”
“A promise that's enforceable.”
He smiled. “Okay.” One more small kiss to Nisa's forehead as he passed by her — quick, casual, like breathing. Then he left, leaving behind the scent of coffee and warmth still hanging in the air.
Nisa watched the door close behind her husband.

Outside the window, the Palace garden, wet from last night's rain, glistened under the morning sun that had just emerged from behind the clouds. Dewdrops at the tips of the palm leaves sparkled like tiny diamonds.
She took a long breath. Straightened her shoulders.

The burden was still there — the stack of memos, the packed schedule, the shadow of an opposition gathering its strength somewhere out there. None of it went away just because of two cups of coffee and a kiss on the forehead.
But somehow, it felt lighter.
Light enough to keep going.
“Okay, Ngel,” she said, her voice regaining the energy she recognized as her own. “Where do we start?”
Angel opened her folder again, this time with an expression a little more relaxed than before. “From the Islamic Community Guidance Directorate's memo first, ma'am. Theirs is the longest.”
Nisa took her reading glasses from the desk, put them on, and looked at the tablet screen in front of her.
Alright.
Let's begin.
— End of Chapter 4 —
PALACE FULL OF EMBERS
5: Gelora Bung Karno Complex, Jakarta
November 5, 2044, 10:30 AM
Jakarta, on certain days, can become a different city.
Today was one of those days.

The vast field at the heart of the Gelora Bung Karno complex had transformed into something that could only be called a human ocean. A wave, colorful and pleasantly noisy — not the crowding of a protest or a crowded train station, but the kind of density that happens when thousands of people gather to celebrate something they believe in together. Jakarta's sky, usually temperamental during the transitional season, chose to be kind today — stretching out a clear blue canvas, as if it too were celebrating National Family Day.

The aromas drifting through the air were unmatched: the savory smell of kerak telor fresh off the hot pan, the sweetness of half-cooked kue cubit puffing thin steam, the smoke of chicken satay from charcoal grills drifting far past the edges of the tents. Amid it all, the sound of children's laughter as they ran freely across the green grass — children today allowed to forget their gadgets for a moment, running as fast as they wanted with no one telling them to stop. Sound from the main stage alternated between announcing winners of the happy family competition and playing family-themed pop songs that got a few mothers swaying lightly while holding colorful plastic umbrellas.

Dozens of exhibition tents stood in neat rows — from ministries, non-government organizations, to grassroots communities from all corners of the country. Stalls of unique handicrafts, organic local food products, free family consultation services from psychologists and marriage counselors, a children's storytelling corner that was always packed.

On the main stage, a woman had just finished her speech. Loud applause from the front rows — some even stood, especially from the women's activist groups and young families who had secured their strategic positions near the stage since morning. The speech was, as always, a blend of a mother's warmth who understood the pulse of family issues and the sharpness of a leader unafraid to point to the root of the problem. She spoke of equal communication in households, the importance of supporting a partner's dreams, and — in the part that made several officials in the VIP row exchange glances — mental, emotional, and financial readiness before a couple decides to have children.
Nisa Farha never gave a speech without touching on something uncomfortable for at least one group present. This was not accidental.

Now she walked among the crowd, escorted by several presidential guard members with flat expressions but constantly moving eyes, accompanied by Angel who faithfully carried a small notebook in her left hand. Nisa was never the type of official who kept her distance — she stopped to listen to a young mother's complaints about how hard it was to find a trustworthy babysitter. She crouched down without hesitation to match the height of a shy little girl with a pink ribbon offering her a drawing of a sunflower. She even laughed freely when a thick-mustached man with a thick Javanese accent asked her to raise the pension allowance for low-grade civil servants.
This was the Nisa who was loved and who also sometimes made the protocol team's breathing go irregular — warm, approachable, deeply real.

After several minutes of direct interaction, Nisa planned to visit a few of the featured craft stalls. She glanced to the side — to where Reza usually stood, slightly behind her, the supportive shadow that was always there.
The spot was empty.
Only Mas Anto, her trusted presidential guard aide, stood there, gaze fixed straight ahead.

Nisa's brows knit together. A small furrow appeared between them. Her eyes scanned the crowd quickly — searching for a familiar figure, black hair graying at the temples, a posture that always looked relaxed wherever he stood.
Nothing.

There are other guards watching him, of course, Nisa thought, trying to suppress the anxious tone starting to creep in. This isn't an emergency. This is just a husband tempted by something in the crowd.
But for some reason, her heart still added a beat or two.
“Mas Anto,” she called quietly, keeping her tone flat. “Where did you last see him heading?”
“Yes, ma'am,” Mas Anto answered professionally. “He was last seen near the craft stall area, about ten minutes ago. Let me check through internal comms.” He spoke briefly into his earpiece.
Nisa nodded. Trying to look relaxed. Not entirely successful, but enough not to alarm those around her.

Probably tempted by the free kerak telor at the Betawi stall earlier. She almost smiled imagining it. Or — more likely — caught up with a crowd of fan mothers wanting photos, and Reza, with his soft-hearted nature, couldn't say no to a single one.

That last thought made her both a little amused and a little guilty. Had she been forcing Reza to always be by her side at events like this? Reza was her biggest supporter, but Nisa knew well that her husband actually preferred the calm of his art studio or the library over the noise of large public events.
Just as she was about to ask again, a voice came from behind her right. Deep. Warm. Very familiar.
“Sweetheart…”
Nisa spun around as if pulled by a magnet.

And there, only a few meters from where she stood, in front of a wood craft stall from Jepara — Reza stood with a wide smile that showed not the slightest awareness he had just made his wife nearly send an emergency signal to the entire security team.

In his hands, he held a miniature Pinisi ship. The carving details looked fine and extraordinary — its sails unfurled as if ready to set sail, its ornaments intricate and full of philosophy. He had just finished talking with an elderly craftsman in a white peci whose face was calm, full of the wrinkles of experience, a conversation that had clearly captured Reza's attention in the way only things that genuinely interested him could.
A wave of relief flooded Nisa — so strong her knees felt slightly weak.
Immediately followed by an equally large wave of exasperated affection.

“Oh my gosh, Pa!” Her voice came out a little louder than she intended. A few people nearby turned with smiles that recognized this situation — the universal scenario of one partner disappearing and the other panicking. “I've been looking for you everywhere, you know! Like searching for a lost kitten at the market!”

Reza looked slightly startled, then chuckled realizing his “sin.” He carefully set the Pinisi miniature back on the display table, then stepped closer. His arm wrapped around Nisa's waist, pulling her into an embrace that felt like an apology, a hug, and protection all in one motion.

“Hehehe, sorry, love. Made you worry?” he whispered, only for Nisa's ears, his eyes looking at his wife with proportionate understanding and guilt. “I accidentally saw this ship carving — the detail is extraordinary. And the craftsman told me the philosophy behind each motif. It was really interesting, so… I lost track of time.”
Nisa shook her head, trying hard to keep her annoyed expression.
Total failure.

A wide smile had already bloomed on her lips. The relief was too great to hide, no matter how much she wanted to still look a little annoyed. “I thought you'd actually wandered off to some herbal tonic stall, or gotten abducted and hauled off by aliens in a UFO,” she joked, repeating one of the ridiculous scenarios that had crossed her mind while panicking.

Reza laughed harder — a laugh that shook his shoulders. “No way, love. How could I ever disappear from your radar? Especially get abducted by aliens.” He tightened his arm around her. “They're scared of you.”
“Ugh, Pa!”
He pulled Nisa slightly away from the crowded stall, finding a quieter gap amid the sea of people. His tone shifted slightly — deeper, softer, shedding his playful layer.
“Sweetheart,” he called, making sure Nisa looked directly into his eyes. “Listen to me for a moment.”
There was something in the way Reza said that sentence that always managed to make Nisa stop — stop from all the noise outside and inside her head, and just focus on this man.

“I know,” Reza continued, his voice calm and sincere in a way that never felt like a speech, “I often look like I'm just following you wherever you go. And maybe sometimes I really am just in the background — behind the spotlight, behind the stage.” His free hand moved gently to touch Nisa's arm. “But for me, that's not a burden. It's a choice. Because the most important thing for me is being able to support everything you do — as president, as a mother, as the woman I respect most in my entire life.”
He paused for a moment.

“This isn't just about you, Sa. It's about us. About our family — even if it's just the three of us with that sometimes-annoying Alex,” a small smile appeared at the corner of his mouth, “but even bigger than that, it's about this country. I'm so proud of you. Of everything you're fighting for, of your courage to break down things considered taboo for the good of millions of people you've never met personally but fight for as if you know each one of them.”
His eyes looked directly into Nisa's. “So — never worry that I'm not here for you. Never feel alone. I'll always be here. Beside you, behind you, wherever you need me.”
Nisa's eyes felt hot.

This always happened when Reza talked like this — no pretense, no phrases that sounded quoted from a greeting card. Just direct words that felt like a truth she'd long held but had just now been said out loud. Her defenses crumbled under that sincerity — all the exhaustion from the long week, the pressure that never truly stopped, the small doubts that often came at three in the morning.

“Thank you so much, Mas…” she whispered, her voice slightly trembling. She rested her head on Reza's shoulder for a moment — an intimate gesture she rarely allowed in public like this, but today she was too tired to care about protocol.
Reza rubbed her back gently.
“We're a team,” he whispered. “A solid team. Storm-proof.”
“Yeah.” Nisa nodded against his shoulder. “A team for our family, a team for this country.”

For a few seconds they stood like that amid the bustling crowd of GBK moving around them — two people momentarily creating their own private space in the middle of a public sea. A few passersby glanced over and smiled. A few photographers on site raised their cameras reflexively.
Then Nisa lifted her head. Took a breath. Straightened her shoulders.
“Okay,” she said, her tone regaining something more upright. “Want to check out the craft stalls together?”
Reza held out his hand. “Let's go.”

They walked hand in hand, strolling along the busy row of craft stalls. Reza stopped briefly at the Pinisi stall to introduce Nisa to the elderly craftsman he'd been talking to earlier — the man looked nervous meeting the First Lady President, but his face brightened when Nisa asked with genuine interest about the philosophy behind the carving in his hands, not just as small talk.

“This is a Pinisi ship, Madam President,” the craftsman explained, his voice warm and slightly proud. “The Bugis people say this ship symbolizes pa'nessa — the courage to sail into unknown seas. Going without knowing what's on the other side, but staying brave anyway.”
Nisa gazed at the miniature for a long moment. “I'll buy one, sir,” she said finally.
Reza beside her smiled.

They walked on, hands still clasped. Nisa was buying a piece of ikat weaving from a Flores craftsman who was explaining the meaning of each motif, when from the corner of her eye — on the right, under a VIP tent guarded more tightly than the others — something caught her attention.
A man.

Standing among two or three sharply dressed people who seemed to be reporting something to him. In his sixties, an upright posture that had never lost its politician's arrogance, a gray suit too neat for an outdoor event.
Hardiman Suryo.

Chairman of the United People's Party faction. The strongest opposition figure who had consistently criticized every significant policy of Nisa's for almost three years — not just in official forums, but often with personal attacks that went beyond policy discussion. The man most frequently quoted in the media with words like “President Nisa doesn't understand Indonesian family values” and “these policies are dangerous to the nation's moral resilience.”
He wasn't looking at the tents around him. Not paying attention to the running children or the busy craft stalls.
He was watching Nisa and Reza.
His gaze was flat and cold — not the gaze of a neutral observer, not someone glancing by chance. This was the gaze of someone weighing things. Calculating. Storing information for later use.
Nisa felt an uncomfortable jolt in her stomach. The old instinct of a politician who had too often been a target.
She didn't look away hastily. Didn't show that she noticed. Simply continued her conversation with the Flores craftsman, finishing the transaction, thanking him warmly. Everything proceeded normally.
But her hand gripped Reza's more tightly.
Reza, sensitive to even the smallest change in pressure in Nisa's grip after nineteen years of unconscious practice, glanced over briefly. His gaze followed the direction Nisa's eyes had caught.
He saw Hardiman.
Hardiman saw Reza seeing him.

A three-way glance that lasted only two seconds but felt longer. Hardiman didn't look surprised — he looked like someone who had been there longer than they realized, waiting for a moment like this. Then he turned back to the people around him, continuing his conversation, as if nothing had happened.
Reza led them away with a casual pace, unhurried, giving no impression that anything was happening. “That was,” he said quietly, only for Nisa, “Hardiman.”
“I know.”
“He's been here a while.”
“I know.” Nisa glanced briefly toward the next stall, her face staying bright for anyone watching. “Let him be.”
Reza nodded. Held Nisa's hand.
They kept walking.

From the crowd on the other side, a faint remark drifted over — its tone cynical, the tone of someone who either didn't care or wanted to be heard. From a group of women looking their way with an expression that couldn't be called friendly:
“…a presidential couple, holding hands and being all lovey-dovey in public like that, not much dignity being kept…”
Nisa heard it.
She didn't show that she heard it.

She knew this was a paradox she'd long been familiar with — the warmth and openness of her affection with Reza was something loved by millions online and hated by certain groups who considered it too liberal, too informal, not “presidential” enough. There was no way to win both at once. And she had long since chosen not to try.
She tightened her grip on Reza's hand.
Refusing to let Hardiman's cold stare or that cynical whisper steal even a millimeter of this moment.
“Za,” she said quietly, “what did the Pinisi craftsman say earlier? About pa'nessa?”
Reza thought for a moment. “The courage to sail into unknown seas. Without knowing what's on the other side, but staying brave anyway.”
Nisa nodded slowly.
“Yeah.” She looked ahead, toward the sea of people continuously moving before them. “Sounds familiar.”
Reza chuckled. “Very familiar.”
They walked forward, hand in hand, stepping into the bustling human ocean beneath Jakarta's blue sky, which today had chosen to be kind.
Behind them, under the VIP tent, Hardiman Suryo whispered something into the ear of the person beside him. That person nodded, then typed something on their phone.
A storm was gathering.
But for now, the Pinisi ship still sailed on.
— End of Chapter 5 —

6: Situation Room, Istana Negara
November 8, 2044, 9:00 AM

Unlike the formal grandeur of the Cabinet Meeting Room or the glitter of the Credential Room, the Palace's Situation Room radiated an aura of cold, efficient functionality. The room wasn't very large — dominated by a long oval table of light wood with a clean surface, surrounded by a dozen or so black ergonomic chairs promising comfort for hours of discussion. The walls were lined with neutral gray panels, fitted with several large monitor screens now displaying various demographic charts, social data, and trend graphs. A large window on one side showed a slice of the Palace's fresh green garden, its vertical blinds drawn half-closed.
The air felt cool. There was a thick sense of anticipatory energy.

At the head of the table, President Nisa Farha sat upright. Her posture radiated calm, but her gaze was sharp and fully focused. A cup of warm jasmine tea — her morning ritual — released a thin wisp of steam beside her. To her right, Angel Marina sat alert with a tablet in front of her. To her left, Anton Prasetya — special staff for social affairs, a walking data analyst who always had a number for every argument — arranged documents with movements that showed he'd read everything since dawn. At the other end of the table, Dr. Haryati Sulaeman, a senior constitutional law expert from the State Secretariat, opened her thick notes with the demeanor of a professional who hadn't come to agree, but to test.
This morning, Nisa needed both.

“Alright,” Nisa opened without preamble, her voice calm but weighted. “Let's continue from where we left off last week. The Family Readiness Bill.” She gestured to Angel, who immediately displayed the proposal's broad framework on the main screen. “This morning I want us to stop talking about whether — and talk about how. The wheels are already turning. Now let's make sure they don't come off along the way.”
There was a second of silence. Then Dr. Haryati opened the discussion.

“In concept and noble intent, this is a breakthrough that's badly needed,” Dr. Haryati said, offering initial appreciation with the tone of an academic who never praises without a caveat. “But from a constitutional law perspective, the challenges will be extraordinary.” She opened the first page of her notes. “First: formulating the definitions of 'measurable mental readiness' and 'basic financial independence' into precise, objective, non-discriminatory statutory language — that's an extremely complex task. We must ensure this definition isn't easily abused or open to multiple interpretations in court.”
“I expected as much,” Nisa nodded. “Go on.”

“Second, and this is the most crucial: potential lawsuits to the Constitutional Court.” Dr. Haryati set down her pen. “Opposing parties will certainly bring this with arguments of violating the fundamental right to marry and form a family, violating individual privacy, and state intervention into customary or religious law. The battle at the Constitutional Court could be harder than the battle in Parliament.”

Anton followed immediately. “Social and political resistance is also certain to be massive and organized, ma'am.” He tapped the report in his hands. “Conservative groups from various religious and traditional backgrounds will unite. Opposition politicians — especially Hardiman Suryo and his faction — will make this easy ammunition. Narratives like 'the state is interfering too much in family matters,' 'the government is making it harder to practice the religious duty of marriage,' 'a secular liberal agenda trying to destroy Indonesian families' — all of that is just waiting to be stirred up on social media.”

Angel nodded in agreement from her corner of the table. “Media framing will greatly determine public perception, ma'am. If we're not proactive from the start, this bill could easily be framed as an 'anti-marriage' or 'anti-religion' policy. Public sentiment could turn negative very quickly.”

Nisa listened to all of it. No anxious furrow on her forehead, no visible tension in her jaw. Her face remained serious, but her gaze grew only more focused — like someone growing more certain, not more shaken, as the challenges piled up.

“I'm fully aware of all the risks you've laid out,” she said after a pause of a few seconds. “And I deeply appreciate the honesty of this analysis. Precisely because we know the storm will be this big, our preparation must be far more mature, more detailed, and more solid.”

She looked at Dr. Haryati. “Bu Haryati, I need a strong internal legal team formed immediately at the State Secretariat. Conduct an in-depth study of every potential legal loophole. Find international precedents from countries that have tried something similar. Most important: formulate the strongest, least legally biased operational definition for that standard of mental and financial readiness. Involve the best psychologists, sociologists, and anthropologists we have.”

She turned to Anton. “I need data as comprehensive as possible as ammunition. Divorce rates, domestic violence, child marriage — their correlation with economic level, education, maternal and child health, and their impact on national productivity. Also map every possible rejection argument — religious, cultural, social, economic, all the way to practical politics. We need fact-based counter-arguments ready for every point of rejection. Don't let this debate be dominated by emotion and sentiment alone.”

“Angel.” Nisa looked at her communications assistant. “Start designing an integrated multi-platform communication strategy. We need to proactively shape a positive narrative from the very first second this draft leaks to the public. Focus the message on its core purpose: protecting our children, empowering Indonesian women, building stronger families. Simple language, easy for ordinary people to understand. Involve influencers, public figures, and civil society organizations who support this issue to amplify the message.”
She leaned back in her chair for a moment, looking out the window. The morning sun was rising higher, its light streaming in.

“This is going to be a long, exhausting fight,” she murmured, more to herself. “Maybe the hardest one of my term so far.” She looked back at her team. “But I'm as certain as I can be — this is a fight worth waging together.”

Silence settled over the room. Not an empty silence — this was a silence filled with a mix of admiration for their leader's vision, awareness of the weight of the task ahead, and a quiet commitment to give their best.
“Any other questions?”
None.
“Then — let's get moving.”
Istana Negara Back Garden, 5:00 PM

The scent of wet earth from the heavy rain that had drenched Jakarta that afternoon rose fresh into the air, mixing with the soft fragrance of jasmine and ylang-ylang climbing the pergola near the back terrace of the Palace. The evening sky at the western horizon refracted a dramatic wash of orange, purple, and pink, reflecting softly on leaves still hung with droplets of water.

Nisa walked slowly along the garden's winding footpath between beds of roses and lush clusters of heliconia. Beside her, Reza — his hand holding Nisa's fingers with a warmth that had never changed in nineteen years.

She had already told him everything over afternoon tea — the bill's three pillars, the rejection arguments the team had mapped out, the instructions she'd given. Reza had listened the way Nisa had long since memorized: fully focused, never interrupting, occasionally nodding or asking one precisely targeted question.
“So, the wheels have started turning,” Nisa murmured, breaking the peaceful evening silence.
“Good team,” Reza commented. “The right people.”

“Yeah. But I also know,” Nisa's voice softened slightly, losing one layer of the firmness she always wore in the Situation Room, “this won't be easy. There'll be a lot of opposition. Misunderstanding. Maybe slander.” A pause. “Maybe a lot of people will hate me for this.”
Reza stopped walking.
He gently pulled Nisa's hand, making her stop and face him. Both his hands cupped her face — his thumbs gently stroking her cheeks in a motion that felt like the most natural thing in the world.
“Hey,” he said. Not loud, never loud. “Listen to me.”
Nisa looked into his eyes.

“Since the first day you decided to run for president, we already knew the consequences. We already knew that being a leader of change in a country this big and this complex means there will always be people who love you and people who don't.” His hands didn't move from Nisa's face. “Especially when you dare to touch an issue this sensitive — about family, marriage, tradition, religion. Something rooted for hundreds of years.”
He paused for a moment, making sure every word landed where it should.

“Will there be hatred? There certainly will. Will there be people attacking you personally, trying to bring you down by any means? Very likely.” His eyes didn't move from Nisa's. “But look at me. I will never be in their ranks. I'm here. Beside you. Always.”
Nisa's eyes felt hot.

This always happened. Reza never gave excessive praise, never said things that sounded like a generic emotional-support script. What he gave was always precisely targeted — words that felt like a truth he held with utmost seriousness.
“I know, Mas,” she whispered. “I know.”
“But,” Reza continued, his tone shifting slightly — the protective layer that occasionally appeared beneath all his warmth and humor. “There's one thing I need you to promise me.”
Nisa waited.

“Take care of yourself,” he said, earnestly. “I know you're strong. I know you're a true fighter. But this fight is different — it's going to drain you completely, Nisa. Not just physically, but especially mentally and emotionally. Don't let this fight eat away at you until there's nothing left. Don't forget yourself in the middle of all this pressure.”
His voice trembled slightly at the end. Not weakness — depth.
“I need my Nisa to stay whole, stay healthy, stay happy. Whatever the final outcome turns out to be.”
Nisa rested her head on Reza's chest. Breathing in the scent of his cologne mixed with the smell of wet earth after rain — a combination she'd associated with the word safe for nineteen years.

“I promise,” she whispered. “I'll try to keep my balance. I won't let this destroy me.” She lifted her head slightly, looking at Reza. “And I'll be okay… as long as you're always beside me like this.”
Reza took her hand, holding it tightly.

“Besides,” he added, a thin smile appearing at the corner of his mouth — the trademark smile signaling Reza returning to his normal self after too serious a moment, “our anniversary interview two weeks ago got a lot of positive response. Lots of messages coming in, saying they loved our honesty and warmth. That's proof that the people need a leader who's authentic, who's human, who doesn't put on airs.”
Nisa laughed lightly — a laugh that felt like releasing a long breath. “So I'm supposed to keep being blunt in front of journalists?”
“I said authentic. If being authentic means being blunt, then go ahead.” He shrugged with an innocent expression. “I'm just the pioneer.”
“The pioneer.” Nisa shook her head, but her smile didn't leave.

They stood there for a while in the dimming evening garden — two people who didn't need words to strengthen each other, who had been together long enough to know that comfortable silence is one of the purest forms of love.
In the distance, the call to Maghrib prayer began to sound faintly.
“But still be careful, Sa,” Reza added finally, his tone turning serious again. “The opposition is really consolidating now. They'll look for any opening, however small.”
Nisa nodded. Her face turned forward again — toward the winding footpath leading deeper into the garden, toward a direction that couldn't be seen from here.
“I won't back down a single step,” she said quietly. Not for Reza, but for herself — confirmation of a decision that could no longer be reversed, one too deep to pull back from.
Reza held her hand tighter.
They walked into the dimming garden, while the sky above them shifted from orange to purple to the dark blue that would soon become night.

Somewhere out there, beyond the Palace walls and the city lights beginning to switch on, unseen wheels were beginning to turn. Unspoken plans were being assembled. A force was gathering itself in the distance.
But tonight, in the wet, fragrant evening garden, there were two hands holding each other.
And that was enough.
— End of Chapter 6 —

7: The President's Private Pavilion, Istana Negara
November 15, 2044, Night → The Following Morning
If there was one thing that always managed to heal Nisa from the kind of exhaustion sleep couldn't cure — the exhaustion of being something to too many people for too long — it was nights like this.
No agenda. No cameras. No one waiting on a decision or a signature or a press statement.

Just a quiet pavilion, aromatherapy candles burning low, and Reza absorbed in sorting through their record collection while sitting cross-legged on the thick Persian rug — his back leaning against the sofa near Nisa's feet as she read a Scandinavian mystery novel Alex had given her months ago. Reza's fingers moved nimbly through the album covers, occasionally pulling one out and weighing it before putting it back. The rustle of thick cardboard sleeves became a soothing background, mixing with the stylus needle occasionally touching a record's surface.
“This one,” Reza murmured, lifting an album with a bright yellow cover.
Nisa peeked from behind her novel. Earth, Wind & Fire. She smiled without saying anything and went back to her page.

The next moment, the cheerful chime of a kalimba filled the room — followed by drums and a groovy, iconic bassline, full of an optimism that had never grown stale despite decades passing. September. A tune that always carried something — nostalgia, relief, memories of their awkward but sweet first date at a small cafe that no longer existed.
“Your favorite song,” Nisa murmured from behind her book.
“Our song,” Reza corrected from the floor, his teasing grin audible even though Nisa couldn't see it.
She didn't have time to respond because Reza had already sprung up with an agile motion and held out his hand — a silent invitation too familiar to refuse.
“Come on.”
Nisa closed her novel, marking the page. “I'm really tired, Za.”
“Exactly why. This is the world's most effective cure for tiredness.”
Nisa looked at the outstretched hand. Looked at her husband's face, showing the charming smile she could never fully resist. Then she sighed in a way that meant I give up and took Reza's hand.
They started dancing.

At first it was just simple small sways — hands clasped, bodies swaying left and right following the cheerful mid-tempo rhythm. Their eyes met. Smiles full of relief. In this moment, in this safe space, the heavy burden of the state completely dissolved — tomorrow morning's cabinet agenda, the queue of bureaucratic memos, the shadow of Hardiman Suryo's cold stare at GBK ten days ago.
None of it. Only this.

Reza occasionally pulled Nisa in close suddenly while swaying, making Nisa laugh in surprise. Nisa retaliated by deliberately stepping lightly on Reza's foot, met with an exaggerated little yelp that made them both laugh harder.

When the rhythm rose during the chorus — Ba de ya, say do you remember? Ba de ya, dancing in September — their movements became livelier, freer. Their hand-hold tightening but staying playful, a simple spin Reza led with confidence. Nisa followed gracefully with restrained laughter, her silk pajamas dancing with her.

During the instrumental section, they spontaneously let go of each other's hands. Nisa — who for this moment completely forgot she was the President of the Republic of Indonesia — shook her hips nimbly and playfully the way she used to at her campus dance studio twenty years ago. Reza, not to be outdone, did a funky, relaxed shoulder move interspersed with a few slightly stiff but very enthusiastic James Brown-style foot steps.
They laughed at each other's moves without any shame.
This was the Nisa and Reza no one ever saw.

The peak came when the iconic Ba de ya repeated near the end of the song — they both jumped lightly in place in an almost synchronized rhythm, their laughter breaking free and filling the entire room. Laughter that was truly pure, that had no agenda whatsoever.

They didn't know — couldn't have known — that in the corner of the room, on a small table near the entrance, a household staff member's phone lay forgotten, left behind when she rushed out for a family emergency call. A phone whose record button had been accidentally bumped while setting down a drink tray.
That small lens recorded everything in silence.
Every movement. Every laugh. Every second of the most private, happiest moment meant only for the two of them.
The phone recorded until its battery died and the screen faded to black.

The next morning, Nisa was still half-drowsy when she touched her tablet to read the news summary. She was chewing a spoonful of chicken porridge when a notification from Angel appeared at the top of the screen, marked URGENT in capital letters.
Angel rarely used that label in the morning.
Nisa tapped the link that was sent.
Her tablet screen displayed the front page of a well-known gossip news portal known for its sensational headlines. And that morning's main headline made the porridge spoon in her hand freeze midair.
VIRAL!! EXCLUSIVE! Dance Video of President Nisa & Husband Late at Night Circulates — Forgetting the People for Hip-Swaying? Is It Appropriate?!
Below the headline: a thumbnail showing the silhouette of two people in an intimate embrace.
With hands that suddenly didn't feel like her own, Nisa pressed play.
The screen showed her and Reza. Dancing joyfully. Laughing without a care. Every movement, every spontaneous moment of theirs recorded clearly in high quality from a familiar corner of the room.
The porridge spoon slipped, falling onto the plate with a soft clink.
“Reza.”
Reza emerged from the bathroom with a towel around his neck and hair still slightly wet. His morning smile faded instantly seeing Nisa's face.
“What's wrong?”
Nisa turned her tablet to face him.

Reza's expression changed within seconds. From curiosity, to shock, to disbelief, and finally hardening into something Nisa rarely saw on her husband's face — a cold mask covering very controlled anger. His jaw clenched tight. His eyes narrowed.
They watched together in tense silence.

Their most private moment — laughter meant only for two people, movements meant only for that room — was now playing on a portal read by millions, analyzed, judged, turned into captions and memes and discussion fodder by hands that had never known either of them.
With quick movements, Nisa opened a social media app.
Her instinct wasn't wrong.

#PresidentDancing. #FirstLadySteamySexyDance. #RezaNisaLewd. All of them already dominating the national trending topics list. Her feed was flooded with the same clip, shared thousands of times by anonymous accounts, buzzers, and ordinary people.
The reaction split right down the middle, as always happened in this country when it came to Nisa Farha.

“Oh my gosh so sweet! Finally seeing our leader's human side!” — “EMBARRASSING! The head of state dancing like that? No sense of shame!” — “Relationship goals for real! So goals!” — “Frivolous! Hedonistic! Better to run the country than party around!” — “This is what a modern-day leader looks like, not stiff like a dry cleaning rag!” — “A bad example for the younger generation! Leaders should be serious!”
Nisa set down her tablet. Her hand clenched on the table.
“Unbelievable,” she hissed quietly. Not loud — but there was something in that tone more dangerous than shouted anger.

“That's not what matters right now, Sa.” Reza's voice sounded calm in a frightening way — calm not because he wasn't angry, but because his anger was too great to release as raised volume. His eyes remained coldly fixed on the tablet screen. “Whether it was staff, whether it was hacked, whether it was sabotage — the fact is this video is already out. Already public consumption.” He finally looked at Nisa. “And most important: they'll use it. This isn't just gossip. This is ammunition.”
As if answering those words, a breaking news notification from a political portal appeared on Nisa's tablet. This time the headline was subtler — but no less cutting:
“Hardiman Suryo: 'National Leadership Needs Full Seriousness, Not Just Hip-Swaying in Private Rooms.'”
Nisa slammed her tablet onto the table.

“I knew it!” Her voice came out louder than she wanted. “That old geezer never misses a chance, no matter how small!” She stood, walked a few steps, turned back. There was something behind her anger that felt like fear — not fear of the attack itself, but fear that this attack would drag Reza deeper into the mud she'd always had to face alone.
Reza walked toward her. Said nothing. Just wrapped an arm around Nisa's shoulder from the side.
“Calm down, Sa.” Quiet. “We face this together. Like always.”
But Nisa could feel the tension in the muscles of Reza's shoulder beneath his calm. She knew Reza was hurt too. Also angry.

The days that followed felt like walking under thick storm clouds. Jakarta's sky might still be clear blue outside the Palace windows, state agendas kept running — but there was an invisible gray layer shadowing every step Nisa and Reza took.

Opinion columns titled “Questioning Public Official Ethics in the Digital Age” and “Guarding the Sanctity of the Presidential Office” sprang up like mushrooms. Political talk shows that usually discussed the economy now had juicier topics to chew on. The news portals Nisa read every morning became a minefield she had to navigate carefully.
One night, in the pavilion's family room after a dinner quieter than usual, Reza sat across from Nisa with a tablet in his hand.
Nisa set down her book. “Are you sure you need to come with me on next week's work trip? Your schedule's packed too.”
Reza looked up. “Very sure.”
“I don't want you having to constantly 'escort' me like this, Za.” There was a note of gentle protest in her voice. “As if I need a shield. You have your own things to do.”
“My top priority right now,” Reza answered, setting down his tablet, “is making sure my wife is okay. Especially while she's a target from every direction.”
“I'm okay.”

“I know you can handle this.” Reza got up, walked over, sat beside Nisa. “But, Sa —” he chose his words carefully, like someone who knew he was walking on thin ice. “Maybe for now, we need to be a little more… strategic in how we respond?”
Nisa pulled her hand back from Reza's grip, which he had just taken.
The atmosphere shifted.
“Strategic.” Her voice rose an octave. “You mean I should stay quiet? Stop being myself just because some old-fashioned people don't like me dancing with my own husband?”
“That's not what I meant—”

“Since when does Reza Satria suggest I stay quiet?” Her eyes looked at Reza in disbelief. “Didn't you always say you were proud that I dare to speak up?” There was a hurt tone she couldn't hide. “Or are you starting to agree with them now?”

“I'm proud of you,” Reza insisted, his voice staying quiet. “Very proud. More than you know.” His eyes didn't look away. “But I don't want you constantly getting drawn into their trap. They're deliberately provoking you to react emotionally, then they twist that reaction to bring you down. This isn't about playing safe, Sa — it's about playing smart.”
A heavy silence fell between them.

Not a major fight. No shouting. But perhaps more dangerous than that — a difference in perspective born from different pressures: Nisa wanting to fight back head-on with her blunt style, Reza suggesting a more measured approach because he saw something Nisa perhaps couldn't yet see from where she stood.
For the first time since the video leaked, there was a thin gap between them.
“I'll keep speaking my mind,” Nisa said finally, her voice flattening again. “I won't back away.”
Reza looked at her for a long moment. Then nodded.
“Alright,” he said. “And I'll be by your side.”

Alex, who appeared in Nisa's office three days later looking his usual self — band shirt, worn jeans, the expression of someone who'd just seen something very entertaining — broke the tension still faintly lingering in the air.

“Mom's middle name really is Controversy,” he remarked, dropping onto the teal sofa. “But seriously, Mom — that video actually made a lot of people like you and Dad more. On my feed, the people sharing it with positive comments far outnumber the angry ones.”
Nisa looked at her son. “Are you comforting me or reporting data?”

“Both.” Alex shrugged. “The angry people are loud, but there's fewer of them. The people who like it are just too lazy to argue in the comments.” He tilted his head. “Besides, honestly — that video actually shows something real. Mom and Dad are ordinary people who can laugh and dance at home. For a lot of people, that's more convincing than any state speech.”
Nisa looked at Alex for a long moment.
Sometimes she forgot that this child, born twelve years into her marriage, could see something even her professional communications team needed a long time to formulate.
“You're so much like your father,” she murmured.
Alex rolled his eyes. “Being told I'm like Dad is supposed to be a compliment? The Dad who yesterday had the idea to 'play strategic'?”
Nisa held back her smile, very unsuccessfully.
“Go on, Lex.”
Alex got up with a grin identical to Reza's, and left behind the scent of unsolicited but always on-target thinking.
Nisa looked at the door closed behind her son.
Then she picked up her phone and typed a short message to Reza:
“You were right about the video. A lot of positive response. And maybe… you weren't entirely wrong about the other night either. Sorry if I was too reactive.”
The reply came within thirty seconds:
“You weren't wrong either. I should've been more sensitive about the timing. Jasmine tea on the terrace at 5?”
Nisa smiled at her phone screen.
“Deal.”

Resolve.

Is ensuring every woman has knowledge and independence before entering the gates of marriage a mistake? The room fell silent again. A different silence than before — heavier, fuller of thoughts wrestling inside the head of each person present.

“This bill is not an attempt to make it harder for people to marry. Not at all.” Nisa's tone was now gentler, but had lost none of its strength. “This is our shared endeavor to ensure that every marriage recorded in this country is a marriage that begins with sincere intent, full awareness, mature readiness, and is founded on genuine love. She looked around one last time — sweeping every face, every expression, holding onto them.

A step we need to take together for the future of this nation we love.”

Nisa gave one last respectful nod.
And then — something that never happens at an event of this caliber, something that would be replayed by every national news channel within the next few hours:
There was no thunderous applause.

There was only a dense silence lasting three or four seconds that felt like several minutes — an awkward silence, full of a shock that hadn't yet found its shape — then the sound of applause emerging sporadically, hesitant, not unified at all. Some people in the front row applauded enthusiastically, especially from among women's activists and progressive academics. But more merely clapped perfunctorily as a formality — or didn't clap at all, their faces showing a mixed expression of shock, disagreement, and confusion about how to react.
The whispers that had been held back now sounded louder.

Nisa remained standing upright at the podium for a few seconds that felt long, her face calm, absorbing all of it. She had already suspected this would happen. She had already prepared herself for this. But still, the sound of that non-unified applause felt like something cold touching her chest from within.
She stepped down from the podium.
Right at the foot of the stage stairs, Reza had already risen from his seat.
He approached Nisa. Said nothing — no words needed to be spoken here, under the spotlight of dozens of pairs of eyes and camera flashes striking again. He simply held out his hand.
Nisa took it.
Their fingers interlaced. Reza held it tightly — Nisa's hand felt slightly cold, he noticed. He tightened his grip, transferring warmth.
His eyes looked at Nisa. One look that said everything without a single word: I'm here. We face this together.
Nisa returned the look. Her breathing steadied itself.
They walked side by side leaving the main stage, passing the row of guests, some still frozen in their seats with unreadable expressions. Cameras followed their every step.
Nisa knew exactly what she had just done. She had just thrown a large stone into the middle of a pond — and the ripples it caused had not stopped. Would not stop for a very long time.
But her hand was still held tightly.
And the Pinisi ship, though the wind had begun to blow harder, still sailed on.

Nisa scrolled the tablet screen slowly.

Short videos containing messages of support. Personal testimonies about the importance of marriage readiness — a mother sharing about her younger sister's forced marriage at seventeen, a female student telling about her friend who experienced domestic violence in her first year of marriage, a young father thanking pre-marital counseling for changing how he viewed marriage. Sincere defenses with no political smell, born from real experience.

And reactions to FaktaIndonesia.com's slander — not just emotional defense, but also analyses from independent journalists meticulously dissecting the inconsistencies in the documents claimed as evidence, showing very clearly that this was a poor fabrication.
“And ma'am—” Anton pointed to one specific video, his voice slightly different. Quieter. “This is the most viral.”
Nisa clicked the link.

The screen showed a young woman in a simple hijab. Her face deliberately slightly blurred to protect her identity — but not fully, because she chose to be known as real, not as an anonymous silhouette. Her eyes were clear: the eyes of someone who'd long been afraid and had just found the courage to speak.
She introduced herself with only a name: Sarah.
Not her real name. But a name that had become a symbol — a name Nisa herself had once mentioned in a meeting with her team as a representation of everything she was fighting for.

“I... I want to share my story,” the voice said, trembling at first, then growing stronger. “I got married at seventeen. Not by my choice. Because of family pressure, because 'someone already wanted me,' because people around me said 'better to marry quickly than stay single too long.' I didn't know my rights. I didn't know I could refuse.”
Nisa didn't move. Didn't sip her tea. Just listened.

“That marriage... wasn't happy. For three years I lived in fear. Not physical violence that could be shown to a doctor — but another kind of violence far harder to prove. I had no financial independence. I had nowhere to go. I didn't know there was legal aid I could contact.”
