That the state should be present to protect me.”
“And now I see her being attacked. Slandered. People who never experienced what I experienced, speaking loudly about how marriage should work.”
She paused briefly. Her breathing steadied.

“I can't stay silent. I won't stay silent. Madam President's courage facing that storm — made me realize I have to be brave too. Thank you, President Nisa. Your fight isn't in vain. We stand with you.”
Nisa stared at the tablet screen.

Tears flowed down her cheeks without her realizing it until they'd already reached her chin — tears coming from a different place than last night's. Not from exhaustion. Not from despair. From something older and bigger than both.
From an understanding — something she'd known from the start but now felt in her bones, not just her mind — that this wasn't about herself.
It had never been about herself.

This was about Sarah. And thousands of other Sarahs who might never make a video, never say her name, but whose lives might change because of the legal foundation being fought for in buildings they'd never enter.
Nisa set down the tablet. Wiped her tears with the back of her hand — a quick movement, once, like someone receiving something and immediately moving forward.
Took a long breath.
Straightened her shoulders.

“Okay.” Her voice returned — not the same voice as last night, but more than that. Steadier. More whole. The voice of a leader who had just rediscovered the ground beneath her feet and had no plans to move from it. “We're not done yet.”
Angel and Anton exchanged glances.
Relieved smiles bloomed on both their faces — smiles that had long waited to come out.

“Angel,” Nisa continued, her hand already reaching for her pen, eyes already on the report before her. “Prepare a draft official clarification for tomorrow morning. Straightforward, fact-based, not defensive. We won't spend energy debating fabrication — we'll present facts and let the facts speak for themselves.”

“Anton. Coordinate with the legal team — the report to the Criminal Investigation Agency must go in today, not tomorrow. And prepare all the original transaction data that can prove not one claim in that article has any basis.”
She paused briefly, looking at the two people in front of her who had already started typing their respective notes with the gesture of people who knew exactly what to do.
“And thank you,” Nisa said, more quietly. “For everything you've done these past weeks. I don't always say it, but I know. And I'm never not grateful.”
Angel nodded. Her eyes slightly misty but she chose not to acknowledge it. “We're here, ma'am.”
“We know where this is headed,” Anton added, closing his tablet. “We're not ready to stop.”
When they left, Nisa leaned back in her chair for a moment.
Looked up at her office's high ceiling — a ceiling that had witnessed too many important moments, too many difficult decisions, too many long nights.
Outside the window, Jakarta was already fully moving under a clean, bright morning sun — the kind of morning that felt like permission to begin again.
Nisa reached for her phone. Typed a message to Reza:
“Have you seen Sarah's video?”
The reply came in two minutes:
“Yes. This morning before I left.”
“And?”
“And I'm even more certain my wife will never be able to stop.”
A two-second pause.
“Also: I'm so proud of you. I already said it, but it needs saying again.”
Nisa stared at her phone screen for a long time.
Then typed one word:
“Come home tonight, okay.”
Reza replied quickly:
“Guaranteed. Want to cook something.”
“Cook what?”
“Something good.”
“That definition doesn't help.”
“A surprise.”
Nisa set down her phone with a small smile that had nothing to do with hashtags, or viral videos, or the crisis reports still piling on her desk.
Just a smile because of Reza.
Which was always enough to keep the day going.

The last day before the vote.

On the VVIP balcony, Reza had already been seated since before Nisa arrived.

He chose the front-most seat on that balcony — not because he wanted to be seen, but because he wanted to see. Wanted to witness firsthand every second of what would become one of the most important moments in his wife's career — and perhaps, in his own life.
In his hands, no tablet or phone. Just his own hands, crossed in his lap, waiting.

Good, Reza thought. Save it for later.

Not from procedural compliance. But because everyone, wherever their position stood, wanted to hear what would come out of President Nisa Farha's mouth on this final day.
Nisa stood.
Walked to the podium with a stride neither rushed nor slow — the stride of someone who already knew she had enough time to say everything that needed saying.

She placed both hands on the sides of the podium. Looked at the room. Swept every face she could reach with her gaze — from the opposition row whose faces were already closed with prepared expressions, to the moderate factions whose eyes still held a little room.
Then upward — to the VVIP balcony.
To Reza.
One second. One look. Reza nodded almost imperceptibly — a small nod that said: I'm here. Go.
Nisa turned back to face forward.

“Honorable members of the House,” she began, her voice filling the room in a way that didn't need a microphone to feel present — but there was one. “Colleagues from various civil society organizations, religious and traditional leaders present today. “Sarah.”

“Not her real name. But a name she chose herself when she decided to speak. Nisa took a breath. When she continued, her tone shifted — more direct, harder, but not hard from anger. Hard from conviction.
“We've heard many concerns raised throughout this long process. About customs being disturbed. About religion being offended. About the state interfering too far.”

“And I respect all those concerns. Truly. The diversity of custom and values this nation holds is an invaluable treasure. Religion is the moral foundation I myself hold firmly in every decision I make.”

“So when I'm asked whether this bill contradicts Islam — I ask back instead: which is closer to the true teaching? A woman forced, silenced, stripped of her right over her own body and future? “Is there a single one of our ancestral traditions whose original purpose was to make women suffer, rather than to protect them?”

Nisa shook her head slowly.
“I don't believe that. And I'm certain, in the most honest corner of our hearts, most of us don't believe it either.”

She took a long breath, and when she continued, her voice carried a different weight — no longer merely a legal or religious argument, but something that felt like the most fundamental conviction of her entire being.

“Ladies and gentlemen, allow me to say one final thing, from the deepest part of my heart. Women are the primary source of life's energy and compassion in this world. They are the ones who carry, give birth to, and raise every generation that has ever existed and ever will. When we damage a woman — strip her rights, kill her dreams, steal her future — we don't just damage one individual. We damage the source from which all the goodness and compassion in this world flows. And the impact doesn't stop at one generation. It rolls forward, grows, and falls upon their children, their grandchildren, into a future we can't even imagine today.”
“Protecting women isn't merely social policy, ladies and gentlemen. This is protecting the source of life itself.”

“The Family Readiness Bill isn't about making marriage harder.” Her voice softened again — but lost none of its strength. “This is about ensuring that every marriage taking place in this country is a marriage that begins correctly. With clear intent. With real readiness. With adequate knowledge. And most importantly — with free and conscious consent from both parties.”

“This is not a foreign agenda. This is not a liberal agenda. This is a humanitarian agenda. An agenda rooted in the most universal value of every religion and tradition on this earth: that every human being deserves to be treated with dignity.”
She paused for a moment. Looked once more toward the VVIP balcony — at Reza, sitting upright, his hands clenched in his lap, his eyes not moving from Nisa's face.

In her mind, fleetingly, that memory surfaced again — not about Sarah, but about herself years ago, long before she knew Reza, long before the word “President” ever crossed her imagination. About the nights she sat alone writing Algorithm City, a science fiction novel about a world where love was forcibly stolen by a system claiming to act for the common good — written by a young woman who at the time hadn't dared admit that what she was really writing wasn't an invented dystopia, but her own fear. A fear that nearly became reality.
“I don't stand here today because I want a political victory. I don't need that victory to measure my administration's success.”

“I stand here because Sarah needs to know someone hears her. Because the millions who wrote 'I am Sarah too' need to know someone is fighting for them. Because the daughters not yet born in this country deserve to grow up in a world safer, fairer, more ready to receive them as whole human beings — not as commodities to be traded in the name of custom or economics.”
Her voice trembled thinly at the end of that sentence — not from nervousness, but from an emotion she'd guarded throughout this long session finally finding its gap.

“I beg all the honorable members of the House — when you cast your vote tomorrow, think of Sarah. Think of your sister, your child, your niece or nephew. Think of the generation that will live with the consequences of the decision we make today.”
“Thank you. Wassalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh.”
Nisa stepped away from the podium.
And then — silence.

Not the same silence as after the National Marriage Day speech two weeks ago. This was a different silence — deeper, fuller, like a room absorbing something just spoken and not yet finished digesting it.
Four seconds.

Then the first applause broke from the activists' row in the observer gallery — loud, standing, without hesitation. Followed by members of the coalition factions who had supported from the start, then several members of the moderate factions whose faces showed a decision they'd just made.
Not everyone applauded. Hardiman's opposition row remained seated, faces cold and locked. Hardiman himself didn't move, staring ahead with the expression of someone calculating numbers in his head.
But the applause that was there — not unified, not perfect — felt more genuine than any obligatory applause Nisa had ever received.
From the VVIP balcony, Reza stood.
Both his hands clenched at his sides, not applauding — not the right place for that — but his body stood as the only way he could say something with no words for it.
His eyes met Nisa's for a second.
Nisa nodded.
The message got through.
Outside the building, among the crowd of journalists already waiting, questions had already been prepared. Tomorrow there would be a vote. Tomorrow there would be certainty.
But tonight, in the presidential car moving calmly away from the Senayan complex, Nisa sat in a silence different from all the silences of the past weeks.
Not a heavy silence.
The silence of someone who had said everything that needed saying. Who had stood in the hardest place and hadn't turned her face away. Who had done what she could, in the best way she was able.
The anger she once could only channel through pages of fiction had finally found its real form tonight — no longer in a novel manuscript, but in the pages of law.
The rest — was not in her control.
And for the first time since this whole storm began, that uncertainty didn't feel like a threat.
It felt like relief.

For always.

An unexpected special guest arrived in the form of a young journalist from a well-known teen magazine — the only media invited, at Alex's own request, who was active in his school's journalism club and wanted to give a chance to a fellow professional still learning.
The journalist — a young woman, looking nervous but trying to appear professional, small notepad in hand — approached Alex among the crowd of his friends.

“Happy birthday, Alex! Fifteen now — soon you'll have an ID card and voting rights. Have you thought about it yet, will you follow your mom's footsteps into politics, or your dad's into being a successful businessman?”

From where she stood, Nisa could see that question land on Alex's face — a split second of an expression showing he was slightly startled, but then followed by something Nisa knew very well. The face of someone composing an answer very carefully without looking like he was composing an answer.
An inheritance never explicitly taught.

“Wow, that's a heavy question, Auntie,” Alex answered with a polite smile that wasn't forced. “If you ask me now, honestly I haven't thought that far. Politics seems really complicated—” he glanced briefly at Nisa with a small smile carrying a thousand words, “—and business also seems like a lot of headaches, right, Dad?” he turned to glance at Reza, who laughed.
“For now I just want to focus on studying, Auntie. Graduate high school well, then hopefully get into a good university matching my interests.”
Suddenly Nisa chimed in from where she stood. “Or just become an actor, Lex! Your face is handsome, it'll sell for sure!”
Alex's friends laughed loudly. Alex rolled his eyes to the sky.
Reza chimed in from beside the grill he'd left. “Well, if he becomes an actor he'll compete with Dad's handsomeness, huh?”
“Dad,” Alex answered flatly, “you don't need to worry.”
“Oh?”
“Our handsome standards are different. Lex is younger.”
Laughter exploded louder — including from Reza, who tried to maintain his offended expression but failed completely.

The young journalist, who'd already forgotten half her questions from trying to hold back laughter, tried to get back on track. “But seriously, Alex — whoever succeeds your mom as leader someday, what do you hope for?”
Alex paused for a moment. This time he didn't answer immediately — there was a small quiet moment on his face, a moment that felt older than his age.

“I can only pray,” he said finally, his voice a little different than before — more serious, deeper, but not losing its openness. “That whoever continues the good things Mom has started can make Indonesia even better.” He paused briefly. “And hopefully the political atmosphere can be a little calmer.” A small smile. “Okay, that's it.”
Several friends nearby gave small applause in a way half-mocking but half-genuine.

Nisa, from where she stood, felt something in her chest with no precise name. Not pride in the grand sense. More like… recognition. That beyond everything that had happened these past months, there was one thing unshaken, unworn, untouched by any storm.
Her son.

When the three-tier black forest cake was finally brought to the middle of the garden — Reza carrying it with excessive ceremony that made everyone laugh — and candles shaped like the numbers 1 and 5 were lit, everyone gathered around the table.
Nisa stood beside Reza. Their shoulders touching.
Alex stood in front of the cake with an expression mixing embarrassment at being the center of attention and happiness he couldn't hide.
“What did you wish for?” Reza asked.
“Can't say, Dad. It won't come true.”
“Wish for something sensible, okay,” one of his friends called out from behind. “Not a bank transfer.”
Loud laughter.

Alex closed his eyes for a moment. Nisa watched her son's face in the small but warm candlelight — a face no longer a little kid's face, already beginning to shape itself, holding so many possibilities.
Become whatever you want, Lex, Nisa prayed inwardly. As long as you're happy. As long as you're good. As long as you never feel alone.
Alex opened his eyes.
Blew out the candles at once — one clean breath.
Everyone applauded and cheered.

The sun had nearly set when the young guests began saying goodbye one by one — some picked up by parents, some taking ride-hailing motorbikes in a way that made the Presidential Guard protocol come to terms with the reality that this wasn't a state event. Alex stood at the pavilion door, giving farewells in a way that showed he'd truly been raised right.

After the last guest left and the garden fell quiet again — balloons still floating, party crumbs still scattered on the table — Nisa, Reza, and Alex sat together on the garden bench facing the sun already nearly swallowed by the horizon.
“Tired?” Nisa asked.
“A bit.” Alex stretched his arms. “But happy.”
Reza handed a leftover piece of cake to Alex. Alex took it without protest.

They sat in a very comfortable silence — the silence of three people who didn't need to fill every pause with sound because their mere presence was enough. In the distance, the sound of Jakarta that never stopped could be heard faintly beyond the Palace fence, but here — on this garden bench, among balloons starting to slightly deflate and leftover cake on paper plates — that outside world felt very far away.
“Dad,” Alex spoke without turning, his eyes still on the horizon.
“Hm?”
“Next year Lex wants to seriously research scholarships abroad.”
A brief silence.
“Where to?” Reza asked.
“Germany. There's a really good environmental engineering program there. Lex already read the curriculum.”

Nisa and Reza exchanged glances — fleeting, above Alex's head, who didn't see. There was something in that look: a mix of pride, worry, and acceptance from two parents who'd been together long enough to know their job wasn't to hold back, but to prepare.
“That's good,” Reza said finally.
“Not saying 'that's really far'?” Alex turned, a little surprised.
“Really far,” Reza answered. “But it's good.”
Alex looked at his mother.
Nisa smiled. “If that's really what you want, Lex — we'll research it together. Find the best one. We'll support you.”
Alex nodded slowly. Looked back at the horizon.
“But later when Lex has gone,” he murmured, his tone shifting slightly — quieter, more honest, “you won't be lonely, right? Here?”
Nisa and Reza were quiet for a moment.
Then Reza answered, his tone light but his eyes serious: “We'll get a cat for company.”
Alex rolled his eyes. “Seriously, Dad.”
“We're serious too,” Nisa chimed in. “But that's for later. Right now focus on you first.”
Alex nodded again. This time there was something a little looser on his face — a small burden he might not have realized he was carrying, now set down.
The last of the sun disappeared behind the distant Jakarta buildings.
The pavilion garden lights turned on automatically, giving a warm yellow glow that made everything feel like a photo worth remembering.
Nisa took a long breath.
This, she thought. Among everything that had happened and everything still to come — this is the part that must never be lost. This is what makes it all worth it.

20: Istana Negara, Jakarta
December 2044 — January 2045
There was no single moment marking the start of recovery.

No big dramatic conversation, no scene where both sat facing each other and formally declared they would rebuild what had briefly cracked. Marriage doesn't work that way — at least not a marriage nineteen years lived by two people mature enough to know that big things are rarely resolved in big ways.
Recovery came from small things.
Always from small things.

The first time Nisa noticed it was the tenth morning after the vote — when she came down to the pavilion dining room earlier than usual because she couldn't go back to sleep, and found Reza already there, sitting in his usual chair, with two cups of tea already prepared and his phone lying face-down at the far end of the table.
Face-down. Its screen not visible. Notifications couldn't disturb him.
Nisa stood at the doorway for a moment, watching.
Reza looked up. “Morning.”
“Morning.” Nisa walked in, took her cup. “Your phone.”
“I know where it is.”
“On purpose?”
“On purpose.”

Nisa sat. Sipped her tea. Looked at Reza, who looked back in a way relaxed and demanding nothing — just present, just here, just for these thirty minutes before the outside world started knocking again.
“Whose idea is this?” Nisa asked.
“My own idea.” Reza shrugged. “We've been sitting at the same table too often but each with a screen in front of our face. Feels like keeping strangers company at a coffee shop.”
Nisa laughed softly.
“Thirty minutes,” Reza said. “Every morning. No gadgets, no briefings, no agenda. Just breakfast. Just us.”
Nisa looked at him.

So simple. Too simple to feel like something important. But that was exactly what made it feel important — because consistent simplicity is far harder to maintain than big things that only happen occasionally.
“Deal,” she said.
And that was the beginning.

The thirty-minute no-gadget breakfast ritual held. Even on days when Nisa had to meet at seven in the morning and had to wake earlier than usual, she set aside thirty minutes before the meeting to sit with Reza. Even on days when Reza had a business trip out of town — the ritual still ran, just in video call format done at the same time, each in front of their own breakfast, phone propped on a book to stand upright, hands free.

Angel, who learned about this ritual after accidentally scheduling a briefing at six forty-five and being met with a look from Nisa that couldn't be misread, quickly adjusted. Nothing scheduled before seven-thirty. No exceptions except grade-one national emergencies.
This wasn't an emergency unless the grade one Nisa meant.
The second small thing came more organically.

One night in the third week of December, Reza came home from a fairly exhausting business meeting to find Nisa still in her office at ten at night — not unusual, but the way Nisa was sitting this time was different from usual. Her back wasn't upright like work mode. She just sat, looking out the window, the tea in her hand long untouched.
Reza knocked on the door frame. Nisa turned.
“Want to talk?” Reza asked.
Nisa was quiet for a moment. Then nodded.

That was the difference from before — before, Nisa might have shaken her head, or said it was nothing, or waited until she'd truly collapsed before opening the door. But that night she nodded. Just that. One small nod meaning more than many words.

Reza came in. Closed the door. Sat in the chair across the desk. They talked for an hour — not about strategy or agenda, but about worry over the new law's implementation turning out slower than expected in some regions, about guilt still occasionally arising, about the question of whether the big decisions made all this time had been right.
Reza didn't offer solutions. Didn't try to solve problems. Just listened in a way showing he was genuinely present — listening not to answer, but to understand.
At the end of the conversation, nothing was practically resolved.
But Nisa slept more soundly that night than in weeks before.

“Relationship evaluation meeting” — the name Reza proposed seriously, which Nisa rejected fiercely, which they ended up using anyway because no better name existed — began taking place every weekend on the pavilion's back terrace.

Not a real meeting. No written agenda. No minutes. Just time deliberately set aside — usually Saturday afternoon, two hours, with coffee and light snacks — to sit together and talk about things often submerged beneath routine: how each was doing, what was going well, what wasn't.
The first session was awkward. Reza opened by asking “so, how are you feeling this week” in a tone too formal, making Nisa laugh and say it felt like a counseling session.
“Maybe there really should be counseling,” Reza answered, not entirely joking.
“Maybe there really should be,” Nisa agreed, also not entirely joking.

But they didn't go to counseling — not because they didn't want to, but because they found that the Saturday afternoon session, in their own slightly awkward way not always reaching a clear conclusion, was already enough. Or at least better than nothing.

In the third session, Nisa finally talked about the small frictions she'd felt for weeks but never raised — the lunch canceled without notice, the cold dinner in the fridge. The way messages arrived late or didn't arrive at all. The loneliness that had settled in slowly.
Reza listened to all of it with a face shifting — from not understanding, to confused, to something more serious.
“That was never from me,” Reza said quietly after Nisa finished. “I never canceled that lunch without telling you directly.”
“From Rahmat.”
Two words. But enough to make something in the air shift.

The informal investigation Anton carried out — in a very Anton way, gathering data systematically without anyone asking because he'd already suspected something for a while — didn't take long to confirm what Nisa and Reza had already suspected.
Small patterns too consistent to be coincidence. Messages always slightly altered passing through one particular hand. Schedules always “wrong” in a way benefiting one particular direction.
Rahmat Iskandar.

No dramatic confrontation. No lengthy internal hearing. Nisa considered her options in a cold, measured way — a way that had become her signature in facing situations demanding a big decision without needing a big fuss.
A week after that terrace conversation, a transfer decree came out from the State Secretariat. Brief, formal, leaving no room for double interpretation.
Rahmat Iskandar, effective January 2, 2045, was reassigned as expert staff at the National Archives of the Republic of Indonesia — Bogor branch.
No press release. No announcement. No words about the reason behind the transfer. Just a decree, a signature, and the State Secretariat's stamp.

Rahmat received his letter on an ordinary morning, at his desk in the Palace, unable to rebut anything because there was no formal accusation he could rebut. Just an administrative decision fully within the President's authority to make.
Nisa didn't need to see his expression to know.
The final new rule — never officially announced but applied with consequences — was born from a casual conversation over two cups of Gayo coffee one Sunday morning.
“If there's an important message from me,” Reza said while sipping his coffee, “confirm directly. Always directly. No intermediary for things concerning the two of us.”
“Agreed.” Nisa nodded. “And if something feels off — something that doesn't feel like it's from me — ask directly. Don't keep it to yourself.”
“Agreed.”
“Regardless of how busy the situation is at the time.”
“Regardless of anything.”
They looked at each other.

No signature. No witness. Just two adults who'd been together long enough to know that the strongest promises are made not at an altar, not before a notary, but at a kitchen table with still-hot coffee and morning light coming through the window.
January 2045 arrived feeling different from previous Januaries.

Not because all problems were solved — problems are never truly solved, only change shape and change name. Implementation of the new law still needed hard oversight. The opposition still existed and still had a voice — Hardiman Suryo never truly left the stage, only gathering energy for the next fight. Nisa's schedule was still packed with no sign of changing.
But something was different.

Beneath all of it — at the most basic layer, at the foundation that during yesterday's storm had briefly felt like it would collapse — something had returned whole. Not whole like before the crack, because nothing can return exactly the same after passing through pressure that great. But whole in a different way — more aware, more deliberate, more knowing how easily a good thing can shatter if not guarded.
A fragility that knows itself fragile, and chooses to stay strong.

One morning in early January, Nisa came down to the pavilion dining room and found what she'd already begun to consider normal: Reza already there, two cups of tea, phone face-down at the far end of the table.
But this morning there was something extra on the table — a small cream-colored envelope, placed beside Nisa's cup.
Nisa took it. Opened it.
Inside, a small card with Reza's handwriting she knew so well — slightly slanted to the right, letters round but hurried, the writing of someone whose mind always moved faster than their hand:
“For my wife who never stops fighting — thank you for being willing to fight for us too. Happy New Year. There's still so much we have to go through together. — R”
Nisa read the card twice.
Then set it beside her, took her tea cup, and sat in her seat.
Reza watched her from across the table with a smile demanding no reaction at all.
Nisa returned it with a smile offering no explanation at all.

Thirty minutes passed in a way already becoming a rhythm — light chat jumping between this week's agenda, Alex's plans already seriously researching universities in Germany, and a small debate about whether there was a good movie they hadn't watched yet worth making a Saturday night plan.
No big resolution. No victory declaration over everything that had passed.
Just this.
Thirty minutes. Two cups of tea. One table. Two people.
Enough.

21: The President's Private Pavilion Garden, Istana Negara
February 17, 2045, 7:30 PM
Nisa didn't like surprises.

This wasn't a secret — everyone who knew her well enough knew this. Angel knew this. Anton knew this. Alex had known this since age eight when he once tried to organize a small birthday surprise for his mother and Nisa showed up too early, saw everything from the door, and spent the next ten minutes laughing and apologizing at once.
Reza, of course, knew this.

Which meant that when Reza told her this 55th birthday celebration would only be the three of them — “just simple, the pavilion garden, a small dinner, Alex will cook his pasta that he says is the best in the world” — Nisa believed him completely.
She had no reason not to believe him.

That afternoon, Nisa came home from the office earlier than usual — Reza had asked her to, with a reason that sounded very reasonable: “It's your birthday, Sa. At least come home before the sun sets.” Nisa didn't refuse. She was even a little glad — the past week had felt like weeks, and the thought of a simple dinner in the pavilion garden already felt like more than enough of a gift.

She showered and changed clothes leisurely — a burgundy silk blouse she hadn't taken out of the closet in a long time, a cream long skirt that flowed softly. As simple as could be called elegant without excessive effort.

When she stepped out of the bedroom toward the terrace facing the pavilion's back garden, Jakarta's dusk was at its most beautiful — the western sky streaked orange and pink, and its last golden light fell drenching the garden Reza had transformed.
Nisa stopped.

The garden was surrounded by hundreds of small yellow lights hung among the trees and pergola — lights that weren't there yesterday, that surely needed half a day to install. In the middle of the garden, a long round table covered with a cream tablecloth with an arrangement of fresh red and white roses. Chairs usually scattered were now arranged neatly. Several tall candles in glass containers floated among the flowers.
Alex stood beside the table with the expression of someone trying very hard to look casual and not succeeding — his smile too wide, his posture too upright.

Reza stood in the middle of the garden, wearing a clean white shirt with sleeves already rolled to the elbow — a way of dressing that always looked the most elegant without trying. In his hand, a glass of non-alcoholic champagne — a substitute for an old habit found years ago.
“Happy birthday, love,” he said.
Nisa looked at it all.

The sparkling small lights. The flowers. Alex whose smile he could no longer hold back. Reza standing in the middle of it all so calmly, like someone who had planned this for a long time and was very satisfied with the result.
“Za,” Nisa said finally, her voice not coming out the way she wanted — too soft, too full. “This...”
“Not done yet,” Reza said, his smile widening a little more.

Dinner went in the best way Nisa could imagine — Alex's homemade pasta, surprising everyone including Alex himself, turned out to be genuinely delicious. Spaghetti aglio e olio with shrimp and a little chili, followed by tiramisu from Nisa's favorite patisserie, bought by Reza secretly three days before and hidden in a freezer section Nisa never opened.

The toast Reza gave made Nisa laugh and nearly cry at once — he called Nisa “the strongest romantic-fire partner ever in the history of human civilization,” a sentence followed by Alex's flat stare and comment: “Isn't there anyone in Dad who's a little normal when giving a toast?”
“This kid,” Reza murmured, but his smile didn't leave.

They ate slowly, talking about light things — Alex's increasingly concrete plans for Germany, a movie the three of them watched together but in different locations because schedules didn't allow, so they could only laugh together through a WhatsApp group, and of course memories of Nisa's birthdays in previous years, each with its own oddity.
“The most memorable was the 40th,” Nisa said, sipping her licorice tea. “Remember, Za? The pavilion power went out exactly when we were about to blow out the candles.”
“And the funniest was the 47th,” Reza added. “Alex ordered a cake reading 'Happy Birthday Grandma' because Lex's handwriting was illegible and the store employee misread it.”
Alex rolled his eyes. “Lex already apologized for that, Dad.”
“Never enough.”
“Dad.”
When the tiramisu was finished and the plates cleared away by staff moving very quietly and efficiently, Reza rose from his chair.
“One more thing,” he said.
Nisa looked at him. “Za, you've already gone above and—”
“One more thing.” He repeated it with a tone leaving no room for negotiation, but in a way so friendly it didn't feel like an order. “Lex, you can close your eyes if you want to be dramatic.”
“I'm not being dramatic, Dad.”
“Close your eyes, Lex.”
Alex closed his eyes with an expression showing he very much didn't accept this order but did it anyway.
Reza turned toward Nisa. His eyes sparkled in a way Nisa had known for nineteen years as a sign he was holding something back — something he'd waited a very long time to reveal.
“Remember what you said back when we were young?” Reza asked. “When we watched their concert video on the DVD player that often glitched in your cramped boarding room?”
Nisa was quiet for a moment. “Said what?”

“You said, if someday there was a chance, you wanted to see them live. But not at a big stadium — at a small place that felt personal. Where you could really feel the music, not just watch it from a distance.”
Nisa stared at him.
Reza turned toward the pergola at the end of the garden — toward the light curtain hanging there, which Nisa thought was just decoration. He gave a small signal with his hand.
The curtain parted.

And behind it — in a deeper garden area that had been hidden all this time, which turned out to have been prepared as a small stage with warm lights and arranged musical equipment — stood four people.
Four people whose faces Nisa had memorized from videos she'd watched hundreds of times on a small screen, from album photos whose covers were slightly worn from being held too often.
Andrea Corr smiled at her from behind the microphone.

“Happy birthday, Nisa,” Andrea said — her voice exactly the same as the voice that had for years filled Nisa's earphones and speakers in her quietest, heaviest, most personal moments. “From us to you.”
Nisa didn't move.

For several seconds that felt like several minutes, she sat in her chair with her hands on the table and breath forgetting how to work, staring at four people who should only exist on a screen, who should be on the other side of the world, who shouldn't possibly be in her own private pavilion's back garden on the night of her 55th birthday.
Then the chime of Sharon's first violin intro sounded.
What Can I Do.
And Nisa cried.

Not a small sob. Not drops that could be hidden. But genuine crying — the crying of someone who had held back too much of something with no name, and finally found its shape in something actually simple: beloved music, a night that felt safe, loved people around her.
Reza sat back down beside her. His arm wrapped around her shoulder.
“Za,” Nisa whispered, her tears still flowing, but her lips smiling — a smile she couldn't stop even trying. “This... this is the best gift of my life.”
Reza kissed Nisa's temple gently. “I know.”
“When did you secretly arrange all this?”

“Since four months ago.” His voice was calm, with the tone of someone satisfied. “When that storm was at its heaviest. Because I knew we'd get here, to the other side of that storm, and you'd need something that felt like a reward for having endured.”
Nisa turned to Reza — a face whose every detail she'd memorized for nineteen years, which still managed to make her feel like she was seeing it for the first time.
“You're crazy,” she whispered.
“Very crazy about you,” Reza replied.
Beside them, Alex, who'd opened his eyes since the curtain parted, now sat with his mouth slightly open and a very rare expression on his face: awe without irony.
“This guy,” he murmured finally. “Seriously, this guy.”
What Can I Do played through to the end, Andrea's voice filling the small garden that today became the most magical place Nisa had ever known.
Then without warning, Andrea Corr spoke again from her small stage. “Nisa — Reza told us you've loved this song for a long time. Tonight, we'd like to invite you up here to sing it with us.”
Nisa froze.
“Don't,” she whispered to Reza. “I can't sing in front of—”
“You can,” Reza cut in, his smile unchanged. “I've heard you sing in the bathroom often enough. You can absolutely do it.”
“That's the bathroom, Za, not a stage—”
“Mom.” Alex turned to his mother with a very rare expression — serious, sincere, without any layer of irony. “Go.”
Nisa looked at her son.
Looked at Reza.
Looked at Andrea Corr, still standing on that small stage with the patience of an artist very used to all kinds of audience reactions.
She stood.

Walked to the stage — legs slightly trembling, heart pounding faster than facing even the most grueling parliamentary hearing. Andrea welcomed her with a warm smile and shifted a little from her microphone.
“Do you know the song?” Andrea asked softly.
“Every word,” Nisa answered.
What Can I Do was played for the second time that night.

This time Nisa sang — not perfectly, her voice trembling at the start, strengthening in the middle, and trembling again at the end not from nervousness but from an emotion that couldn't be fully controlled even by a president.
From the table in the middle of the garden, Reza watched her.
Not taking a photo. Not recording a video. Just watching — in the way of someone who had decided to keep this moment not in a camera, but in a place far safer and far more permanent.
Alex, who had taken out his phone to record but then set it down again after seeing his father wasn't recording anything, joined in watching his mother sing beneath the sparkling small lights.

That moment — their mother on a small stage in their own home's garden, singing with a band she'd loved since before Alex was born, beneath Jakarta's clear sky and warm yellow lights — was something he wouldn't tell anyone.
Not because he didn't want to share.
But because some things are too beautiful to share. Some things are only for keeping to oneself.

When the song ended and the small garden filled with applause — staff who had been peeking from behind the door, Alex applauding while whistling, and Reza applauding the longest — Nisa walked back to Reza with a different stride than before.
Lighter.
Like someone who had just set down something she hadn't realized she'd been carrying.
She embraced Reza — not a polite or planned embrace, but a direct one, a tight one, that said everything without a single word.
“Thank you,” she whispered against his shoulder. “Not just for this. For everything.”
Reza tightened his embrace.
“Happy birthday, my Nisa,” he said quietly. “For the fifty-five years that have been. And for everything still to come.”
Above them, Jakarta's sky tonight — for one night only — felt entirely theirs.

At the end of the garden, Andrea, Sharon, Caroline, and Jim still stood on that small stage, receiving thanks from several guests slowly approaching — light chat, laughter, some spontaneous photos clearly violating protocol but no one intended to correct it tonight.
Nisa watched them for a moment from a distance — four faces she'd memorized since she was a teenager with a DVD player that often glitched, now standing real in her own home's garden.
A small, silly thought, very much against any presidential protocol, began forming in her head.
“Za,” she whispered, still leaning on Reza's shoulder.
“Hm?”

“Earlier at dinner, Sharon told me something. They just finished promoting their old album, and filming the music video for their new album doesn't start until next month.” Nisa paused for a moment, as if weighing something not yet fully formed in her head. “Which means... their schedule is open for the next month, right?”
Reza raised an eyebrow, trying to read the direction of that question. “Why? Want to invite them to perform here again?”

“No. Bigger... than that.” Nisa's smile widened in a way that made Reza feel a mix of curiosity and slight wariness — a smile he'd learned to recognize as a warning sign after nineteen years together. “Just thought of something. But if this really goes ahead, I need to talk to Angel first about security, and maybe their manager too.”
“Something like what, Sa?”

“We'll discuss it seriously later,” Nisa said, her eyes still fixed on the four people on that small stage, laughing with Alex about something inaudible from here. “But it seems this year's birthday isn't quite over yet.”

22: The President's Private Pavilion Terrace, Istana Negara
March 2045, 10:00 AM
Three months after the gavel fell.

Life hadn't returned to the word “normal” — maybe it never would, and Nisa had long made peace with that reality. The new law's implementation still needed hard oversight on the ground. Several regions were grappling with cultural resistance stronger than expected. Promised budgets hadn't fully been disbursed. And Hardiman Suryo, though no longer at the front line, still spoke from various platforms in ways subtler but no less irritating.
But something was different from three months ago.

It wasn't external conditions that changed — that storm, in its various forms, would always exist. What changed was how Nisa stood within it. How Reza stood beside her. How they held each other's hand — not from fear of falling, but from choosing to walk together.
The pavilion's back terrace this morning felt like the best version of itself.

The old, leafy garden trees created a natural canopy filtering the morning sunlight into golden fragments falling on the stone floor and wooden table surface. The wind moved slowly, enough to make the white cotton curtains at the terrace door sway a little. The scent of coffee and jasmine tea mixed in the air.

In one corner of the terrace, two comfortable rattan chairs had been prepared — facing the garden, not facing a camera. That was Nisa's request from the start: she didn't want to sit like she was at a podium. She wanted to sit like she was at home.
Because this was indeed her home.

The journalist interviewing her this morning — Dian Kusuma, a senior journalist who'd covered Indonesian politics for twenty years and the only journalist who'd ever managed to make Nisa laugh out loud in the context of a serious interview — sat in a third chair added later, with a small recorder on the table and a notepad in her lap.
Reza sat beside Nisa.
This was a joint interview — something rare, something they didn't often do, but which Dian proposed and Nisa welcomed after no small consideration.
It's time, Nisa had thought then. Not as a performance. But as testimony.

“Madam President, Pak Reza — thank you for making time.” Dian opened with an already-familiar smile, the smile of someone who'd covered long enough to no longer be nervous before a head of state but still respect the moment. “Three months since the Family Readiness Bill was enacted. How are things now?”
Nisa sipped her tea for a moment. “Honestly?”
“Always.”

“Implementation is harder than passing it.” Nisa answered without stalling. “We can make a law in months. Changing a society's mindset formed over hundreds of years — that's a generation's work, maybe two.” She glanced at Reza for a moment, then back to Dian. “But that doesn't mean we stop. Quite the opposite.”
“Pak Reza,” Dian shifted, “you're one of those most personally affected by all this controversy. How does it feel being the 'president's husband' amid a storm this size?”
Reza didn't answer right away. He looked toward the garden for a moment — his habit when searching for the right word, not the easy one.

“There were moments when I felt...” he paused, choosing. “Irrelevant. Not because Nisa made me feel that way — she never did. But because my position is structurally not a position with room in the public narrative. President's husband isn't a role with a job description.”

“But then,” he continued, a thin smile appearing, “I remembered why I'm here. Not because of the title. Not because of the camera. But because this is a woman I love, who's fighting for something right, and who needs someone who believes in her even when half the world doubts her.”
“Did that not feel irrelevant at all?”
“No. It felt like the one most relevant thing there was.”

“There's something I'd like to ask directly,” Dian continued, her tone slightly different — more careful, more personal. “Throughout this long process, there were reports from various sources — none confirmed, but fairly consistent — that there was tension in your and Pak Reza's relationship. That the political storm wasn't just attacking from outside, but also pressing from within.”
A few seconds of silence.
Nisa and Reza looked at each other — a quick glance already long enough to convey something only they fully understood.
Then Nisa turned to Dian.

“Yes,” she said. Simple, direct, without hiding behind diplomatic sentences. “There was pressure. There was a small crack that briefly appeared. There were heavy nights — not just heavy professionally, but heavy as a couple.”
Dian didn't interrupt. Waited.

“The secret of our marriage isn't that there are no secrets,” Nisa continued, and Reza beside her nodded slowly confirming. “It's also not that there are no problems. Not that there are no days when one of us wanted to throw in the towel.” The corner of her mouth lifted thinly. “The secret is — we always choose not to throw that towel in.”
“What makes that possible?” Dian asked.

Reza answered before Nisa could. “Honest communication. Which sometimes hurts. Which sometimes comes late.” He paused for a moment. “And trust that the person beside us, even when wrong or unintentionally hurting us, is fundamentally on the same side.”

“A spouse's victory is a shared victory,” Nisa added. “A spouse's defeat is a shared defeat. No one wins alone in a marriage. If one side wins and the other loses — that's not a healthy marriage, that's a competition.”
Dian noted something down. “And was there a moment when either of you nearly gave up? Not on the political fight — but on the marriage itself?”
A longer silence.
Nisa set down her tea cup. Looked at her own hands for a moment.

“There was a night I sat alone in my office and felt a very deep loneliness,” she said finally, quietly. “Not because Reza wasn't there. But because the pressure we both carried — from different directions, in different ways — briefly made us like walking on parallel paths that never met.” She paused. “And that... was frightening. Because the person I needed most was physically very close, but felt very far.”
“How did you close that gap?”
This time Reza and Nisa answered at the same time — then both stopped and smiled because of it.
“You first,” Reza said.

“By coming,” Nisa said. “In the most literal sense. Reza came. With two cups of tea in the middle of the night. Without much talk. Just present.” Her eyes glanced at her husband. “That's what changed everything.”
Reza shrugged in a way not trying to look humble. “I just did the easiest thing.”
“The easiest thing is sometimes the hardest to do,” Nisa replied.

“One last question,” Dian closed her notebook, a sign she already felt satisfied with what she'd gotten today but still wanted one more thing. “If there's one thing you and Pak Reza want young couples in Indonesia to know from everything you've gone through — what is it?”
Nisa thought.
Reza thought.
This time neither answered simultaneously. Reza gestured with his hand — you first — and Nisa nodded.

“Choose a partner who believes in what you're fighting for,” Nisa said. “Not one who only supports when it's easy. But one who stays — even when supporting you means they also have to bear something heavy.” She glanced at Reza. “That's rarer than you think.”

Reza nodded. “And from my side—” he thought for a moment, “—marriage isn't about having no problems. A good marriage isn't one that never cracks. But one that always chooses to repair its cracks, rather than letting them widen.”
“Like kintsugi,” Dian murmured — a reference to the Japanese art of mending cracked pottery with gold, making the crack marks part of its beauty.
Reza smiled. “Exactly like that.”
Dian said goodbye half an hour later, leaving the terrace with a light step and a full recorder — and the expression of someone who'd just gotten more than what she came looking for.
Nisa and Reza remained sitting in their chairs.

Not moving right away. Not immediately checking their phones or opening their agendas. Just sitting and letting the morning continue in its own way — the sound of birds in the garden, the wind occasionally moving the curtain, the scent of coffee gone cold but still fragrant.
“You don't mind that I was honest earlier about those heavy nights?” Nisa asked finally.

Reza shook his head. “Quite the opposite.” He turned to Nisa. “That's the most important thing for people out there to hear. Not that our marriage is perfect. But that even an imperfect marriage can endure — and more than that, can grow.”
Nisa looked at the garden before her.
In one corner among the trees, a cluster of kemuning flowers was blooming — small, yellow, unremarkable, but their faintly sweet scent could be smelled far beyond their size.
“Za,” Nisa said.
“Hm?”

“Thank you for staying.” She didn't turn — her eyes still on the garden, but her tone conveyed something bigger than her words. “Not just yesterday. Not just during that storm. But every day. Every small choice to stay.”
Reza reached for her hand on the armrest. Held it.
Said nothing.
No need.
The interview article was published a week later in a national magazine with a title Dian Kusuma wrote very carefully after a long discussion with the editor and editorial team:
“Nisa and Reza: On a Love That Chooses to Stay.”

On its publication day, the article became the most shared across every social media platform — not with a hashtag stirring controversy, not with a quote cut to provoke debate. But with short captions written by ordinary people:
“This is what partnership means.”
“Read this crying from start to finish.”
“Please show this to anyone who says marriage shouldn't have problems.”
And one short comment reposted the most, from an account no one knew but everyone felt they recognized:
“Finally someone said out loud that enduring doesn't mean never nearly giving up. Thank you.”

23: The President's Private Pavilion Balcony, Istana Negara
Late October 2048
Four years.
Measured by the toll of the Palace wall clock — four years passed at a speed only understood by someone who's lived it: too fast and too slow at once, depending on which moment is being remembered.

Measured by the depth of the wound once torn open, by the foundation nearly collapsed and rebuilt brick by brick — four years felt like an eternity full of things that couldn't be conveyed in any annual report.

Tonight, their private pavilion balcony facing the Palace garden was bathed in the light of a nearly perfect full moon. The October air felt fresher than usual — the most honest transitional season among all seasons, when Jakarta's usually light-polluted sky occasionally gave room for stars to be seen more clearly.
Nisa stood on that balcony.
The same place where she once stood alone in the predawn hours, accompanied by White Light's melody and the dark shadow of doubt. The same place where too many questions once spun without answers.
But tonight was different.

Reza stood beside her — their shoulders touching, his hand reaching out and Nisa already holding it without needing to be asked. From the terrace below, the sound of Alex on a video call with his friends in Germany occasionally floated up — a mix of Indonesian, English, and German he'd begun mastering in a way that made Nisa unable to decide whether pride or nostalgia was more dominant.
“Remember four years ago?” Nisa asked quietly.
“This balcony?”
“Yes.”
Reza nodded. His smile didn't come immediately — something older appeared on his face remembering those nights. “I remember.”
“Feels so far away now.”
“Yeah.” He held Nisa's hand tighter. “But not gone.”

Four years was enough time to see a law begin working — not dramatically, but in the most honest way: slowly, imperfectly, with many field obstacles never imagined when the first draft was written on the Palace's work desk.
Yet the numbers were there.

Anton, who prepared that four-year evaluation report — forty pages, typically Anton, but this time with tables and graphs that even Nisa, already used to data, still felt a little overwhelmed by. He summarized it in one paragraph when presenting it to Nisa last week, in a tone he didn't often use:
“Ma'am, the numbers speak.”
Early divorce under age twenty-five: down eighteen percent nationally. In provinces with the strictest implementation, the figure exceeded twenty-three percent.

Domestic violence reports coming into legal aid institutions — not down because victims weren't reporting, but down because more couples were entering marriage with more realistic expectations and better communication tools: down twenty-two percent.
Average age of first marriage rose three years compared to before the law took effect.

And what Nisa kept closest to her heart: the pre-marital counseling program, initially rejected outright by various groups, now had a waitlist in several regions — young couples signing up themselves, not because required, but because they chose to be ready.

“The numbers aren't all good,” Anton added honestly. “There are regions where resistance is still very high. There's implementation still just on paper. There's budget not disbursed.” He tapped the last page of his report. “But the direction is clear, ma'am. This is working.”

Nisa kept that report in her desk's top drawer — not among the usual pile of policy documents, but in the drawer holding only a few things: a folded family photo, one sheet of paper with the name Sarah written on it, and that report.
On the balcony tonight, that thought surfaced again uninvited.
“Za,” Nisa said.
“Hm?”
“Have you ever wondered — how is Sarah now?”
Reza knew who was meant. He didn't need to be asked twice.
“Hopefully well,” he answered quietly. “Hopefully she's found a way to live more in line with what she wants.”

Nisa nodded. “I think so too.” A pause. “Sometimes I want to know. But then I realize — no need to know. What matters is the law exists. So whoever comes after Sarah doesn't have to go through the same thing.”
Reza said nothing. Just raised Nisa's hand, kissing its back gently.
The sound from below changed — Alex had finished his video call, his voice now floating up the stairs toward the balcony.
“Mom. Dad. Still outside?”
“Here,” Reza called.

Alex appeared at the balcony door — plain gray t-shirt, hair grown a bit longer since he moved to Germany with no Nisa able to make him cut it, the expression of someone who'd just finished laughing and hadn't fully returned to his normal face.
“Who were you talking to?” Nisa asked.

“Lab friends. There was an experiment result that was really funny this afternoon, so everyone was telling stories.” He leaned against the door frame. “Also got an email from my advising professor earlier. Said Lex's research proposal was approved to be presented at the conference next month.”
Nisa turned to Reza.
Reza turned to Nisa.
Both turned to Alex.
“Seriously?” Nisa said.
“Seriously.” Alex shrugged in a way trying to look casual but not entirely succeeding because something was shining in his eyes.

Nisa got up from her leaning position, stepped toward Alex, and before he could dodge — was already hugged. Tight. The kind of hug only a mother who knows her child is far away can give, making a physical moment like this more precious than before.
“Mom,” Alex murmured, a bit awkward but not pulling away.
“Quiet,” Nisa said against his shoulder. “Let Mom be proud first.”
From his position on the balcony, Reza watched the two people he loved most — his wife unable to hide her happiness, his son trying to look too grown-up to be moved but clearly not succeeding.
He didn't move. Didn't take a photo. Just watched.
Kept it.

After Alex returned to his room — with the excuse of “still a lot of assignments,” which might have been true and might also just be a way to avoid a moment already too touching — Nisa and Reza returned to their spots on the balcony.
Quieter now. Deeper.
“Want to run for a second term?” Reza asked suddenly.
Nisa turned to him. “Where did that come from?”
“It's been in my head a while.” He looked at Jakarta below. “Just now dared to ask.”
Nisa was quiet for quite a while before answering.

“Don't know yet,” she said honestly. “Still much unfinished. This law's implementation alone still needs hard oversight. There's another agenda only halfway done.” She leaned against the balcony railing. “But on the other hand — I also know that tiredness is real. And there are things outside this Palace I also want to live fully, not just in the gaps between schedules.”
“Like?”

Nisa thought. “Like going to Germany and seeing Alex's lab with my own eyes. Like sleeping until nine without feeling guilty. Like reading a book I bought but never opened because there was always something more urgent.”
Reza smiled a little. “Those aren't small reasons.”
“No.” Nisa nodded. “But they're also not reason enough to stop if there's still something that needs finishing.” She looked at Reza. “You yourself — what do you want?”
“Me?” Reza raised his eyebrows. “I already have what I want.” His hand reached for Nisa's hand. “Just need to make sure the person beside me is happy and healthy.”
“That's not an answer.”
“That's the most honest answer I can give.”
Nisa looked at him for a long time.

Then smiled — a smile that existed on no podium, in no official photo. A smile that only lived here, on this balcony, between two people who'd been through enough together to know the most precious things could never be published.
“We'll see,” Nisa said finally.
“Okay.” Reza nodded. “We'll see.”
They stood quietly for a while longer — watching Jakarta continue glowing beneath a sky choosing to show a little more stars than usual tonight.
Not a wild fire burning everything.
Not ash gone completely cold either.
A stable ember — the kind of ember that doesn't need constant blowing to stay alive, that isn't shaken by ordinary wind, that knows how to endure without needing to be dramatic.
A new frequency, Nisa thought.

Not a different tune than before — still Nisa and Reza, still two people who first met at a campus discussion forum twenty years ago, still a couple who more often loved each other through small things than grand words.
But the tempo was different. More aware. More deliberate. More knowing of its worth.
Below, Jakarta's sound kept flowing.
In the room next door, Alex was working on something for next month's conference.
In Nisa's hand, the warmth of Reza's hand that didn't leave.
That was already more than enough for tonight.
And for every night still to come.

24: Jakarta and Surroundings
2048 — Four Years After the Vote
Real change rarely comes with fanfare.

There's no day when everyone stops and says: this is it, this is the moment, this is the point where everything starts being different. Real change works like water seeping into soil — slowly, silently, without announcement. And only after some time, looking back, do you realize the ground is different from before.
Four years after the gavel fell, Indonesia was different.
Not dramatically. Not perfectly. But different — in a way anyone willing to look closely enough could feel.

In a small subdistrict in Central Java, a female pre-marital counselor named Rahmawati — who four years ago worked alone with meager funding from community donations — now led a team of eight counselors funded by the regional budget. Her clients averaged twenty-one to twenty-five years old. They came not because required — the law does require counseling, yes, but Rahmawati knew the difference between people coming to check a box and people who genuinely wanted to learn.
Those coming to her office now were more of the latter.

“Before,” Rahmawati said in a local media interview, “young couples came to counseling with faces saying: this is a formality, let's finish quickly. Now, they come with questions. Serious questions — about finances, about communication, about how to raise children in a way that doesn't damage them. They want to know.” She paused briefly. “That's what changed.”

In Makassar, a man named Hendri — who four years ago nearly forced his daughter to marry his business partner because of family debt pressure — was now one of the local facilitators for the law's outreach program in his community.
Not because he was a different person from four years ago. He was still the same person, with the same pressures, the same tendencies.
But four years ago, his daughter showed him the law's third article. About a child's right to refuse an arranged match. About sanctions for those who force it.

“I was angry then,” he admitted honestly. “Angry because I felt the government was interfering. But my daughter said: Dad, this isn't about the government interfering. This is about me having a right no one ever told me I had.”
He sighed.
“And I couldn't fight that.”
His daughter was now in her third year studying civil engineering. Still unmarried. Still had her own dreams she hadn't finished chasing.
Hendri felt prouder than he'd ever imagined possible.

At a high school in Surabaya, a guidance counselor named Pak Darmawan had spent the last three years integrating a family readiness module into his school's extracurricular program — well before the formal requirement from the education office.
His students, who initially thought the sessions boring and irrelevant, now sometimes came to his room outside class hours. To ask. To share.

“The ones who come most,” Pak Darmawan said, “are actually boys. Who no one wants to talk about feelings and fears with elsewhere. Who were never taught they're also allowed not to be ready. That they're also allowed to say: I don't know yet.”

Anton presented all these stories — not just statistical numbers, but stories — in the presentation he prepared for the year-end evaluation meeting. Forty pages of formal report, but in the last section, ten pages with no tables or graphs.
Just stories.
Rahmawati. Hendri. Pak Darmawan. And several other names whose permission had been asked, identities protected as they requested, but whose stories were real and verifiable.
Nisa read those ten pages twice.
Then set the report on the desk and sat still for several minutes — not out of a loss for words, but because sometimes words don't feel big enough to hold what's being felt.

This. This is where it all made sense — not in the plenary chamber, not on the trending board, not on Hardiman Suryo's cold face. In a small counseling house in Central Java. In a conversation between a father and daughter in Makassar. In a school guidance room in Surabaya whose door was always open.
There.
The President's Office, Afternoon
When Angel and Anton came in for the brief evaluation session — their way now: more relaxed, more like conversation than formal briefing — Nisa was already ready.
“That eighteen percent drop in early divorce,” Nisa began, “I want to know: where is the impact most felt? Which region?”

Anton answered without needing to open his notes — a sign he'd memorized it. “West and East Nusa Tenggara, ma'am. Which have historically had the highest early marriage rates nationally. There the drop was twenty-three percent.”

“Implementation there wasn't easy,” Angel added. “There was very strong traditional resistance at first. But traditional leaders who eventually sat with us — three or four people who truly changed the narrative direction in their communities.”
Nisa nodded. “Are their names recorded?”
“Yes, ma'am. In the report appendix.”

“I want a formal recognition for them this year. Not from the Ministry, not from Parliament. Directly from the President's office.” Nisa turned to Angel. “Something personal. Not just a plaque and photo.”
Angel noted it. “Yes, ma'am.”
Reza, sitting on the corner sofa with a cup of coffee and a book he hadn't really been reading, looked up. “The domestic violence numbers?”

“Reports coming in down twenty-two percent,” Anton answered. “But more important — access to legal aid services up three hundred percent. Meaning it's not fewer victims, but more who finally dare report and get help increasing sharply.”
Reza nodded slowly. “That's the more important one.”
“Far more important,” Nisa agreed.

There was a comfortable silence in the room — the silence of four people who'd worked together long enough not to need to fill every pause, who knew that quiet is sometimes the best way to let something just conveyed fully sink in.

“There's still a lot unresolved,” Nisa said finally. Not as pessimism — as a fact she accepted calmly. “Resistance in some districts is still high. Implementation budget in remote-frontier-disadvantaged regions is still far from ideal. Trained counselors are still lacking.” Her eyes scanned the room. “This isn't the time to be satisfied.”
“But?” Angel already knew Nisa's speech patterns well enough to know there was a but.
Nisa smiled thinly. “But the direction is clear. And that — after everything we've been through — that's not a small thing.”
That small celebration happened not because it was planned.

That afternoon, after Angel and Anton left, Nisa found Reza still on the same sofa, but his book was closed now. On the small table beside him were two cups — Gayo coffee for himself, jasmine tea for Nisa — and a small box from their regular patisserie.
“What's this?” Nisa asked.
“Chocolate sprinkle donuts.” Reza opened the box in the way of someone who'd been keeping something and was very pleased with himself. “Which you said you hadn't had time to eat since... whenever.”
Nisa looked at the box. Looked at Reza.
“Za, this is—”
“Not a big celebration,” Reza cut in. “Just donuts. And two people who deserve to eat donuts after four years.”
Nisa sat beside him.
Took a donut. Bit into it. Her eyes closed for a second — not dramatic, but sincere, the way of someone just realizing how long it had been since she'd done something this simple.
“Reza.”
“Hm?”
“This is really good.”
Reza laughed — a deep, genuine laugh, the laugh of someone with no other agenda besides this moment.
“Yeah,” he said. “I've been saying that all along.”

They ate donuts on the sofa of the President of the Republic of Indonesia's office on an ordinary afternoon — no camera, no agenda, no one knowing except Mas Anto standing outside the door, already well trained never to tell anyone about things like this.
Two people who'd been together long enough to know that true happiness never needs an audience.
Outside the window, Jakarta moved the way Jakarta always moved — without stopping, without asking permission, without caring about what had just been finished or what was still waiting to begin.
But on that sofa, for twenty minutes that would never appear in any news — there was light.
Not a blinding light. Not a light needing to be announced.
A small, warm, stable light.
The hardest to get, and the most precious to keep.

October 30, 2048
Twenty-three years.

Today, twenty-three years ago, Nisa Shabrina Farha and Reza Satria stood before the marriage officiant with slightly trembling hands and smiles not knowing how to hide their nervousness. No one present that day would have guessed that young couple would end up here — at Istana Negara, on this balcony, beneath Jakarta's sky choosing to be more beautiful than usual tonight.
Or maybe the sky was the same. Only the way of seeing it had changed.
No press conference today.

Nisa decided that from early October — the 23rd anniversary belonged to them, not to the public. Enough already, previous years with camera flashes and questions about the secret to a lasting marriage. This year, just the two of them was enough. And Alex, who flew home from Germany specifically for three days.

Alex, now twenty, whose height definitively surpassed Reza's now and who never stopped reminding him of that, whose Javanese accent now mixed with a funny German-English accent, who had slept twelve hours since landing yesterday because of jet lag he dramatized more than necessary.
Night fell calmly.

In the pavilion garden below their balcony, small lights Reza had set up since afternoon sparkled among the leaves. Not the same lights set up for Nisa's birthday party three years ago — simpler, more personal. Just a few hundred small points of light creating an atmosphere needing no words to explain.

On the terrace table: two glasses of apple juice. One small box from their regular patisserie — chocolate truffle cake, not a grand celebration cake. And a small portable music player Reza had already connected, its playlist ready.
Nisa stood at the balcony railing, looking at the city below.

Jakarta at night — millions of lights never fully dying, the pulse of a city too alive to sleep. She'd looked at this view hundreds of times from this same balcony, from moments very different from one another.
Nights when she stood alone with questions with no answers.
Nights when Reza stood beside her and those questions felt lighter just because someone was willing to bear them together.
Tonight.
Which felt — different from all of them.
Reza appeared from the balcony door, carrying two glasses of apple juice. Set one in Nisa's hand, already automatically reaching out, and stood beside her.
“Alex asleep again?” Nisa asked.
“On the sofa. Holding the TV remote.” Reza sipped his juice. “Less than three minutes ago.”
Nisa giggled. “Still same as always. If he doesn't accidentally fall asleep, he's not Alex.”
A comfortable silence fell between them.
Not a silence needing to be filled. The kind of silence they knew very well — a silence that emerges when two people have been together long enough to know presence can speak louder than words.
Below, the pavilion garden sparkled in small, warm lights.
Reza took the music player from the terrace table. Pressed play.
What came out wasn't Miles Davis or Earth Wind & Fire or The Corrs.

What came out was something different — an instrumental composition Nisa didn't immediately recognize. Its melody flowed in a way that felt like a fusion: a touch of calm ambient, a simple melody that felt a little like an Irish fiddle, a beat almost imperceptible but there.

Reza smiled. “My own making.”
Nisa turned. “When?”

A mix of music we each like — the ambient part from me, the melody inspired by The Corrs you love.” His smile was a little shy, a way he rarely showed. “Not perfect yet. But I thought, tonight was the right time for its first play.”
Nisa listened.
Truly listened — not with ears processing information, but with a way of listening older than that.
The melody flowed. Simple, not complex, but with a depth that only emerges from something made not to be heard by many people but for one person alone. Or two.
“Za,” Nisa said quietly.
“Hm?”
“This is beautiful.”
Reza didn't answer. Just held out his hand.
Nisa welcomed it — fingers interlacing in a way that had become muscle memory for twenty-three years, a way never needing thought but always feeling like coming home to the most fitting place.

“Have you decided?” Reza asked finally. His tone light, not demanding — he knew this question didn't need answering tonight.

“It's the only honest answer.”

“Dad, Mom — breakfast outside tomorrow, okay? Lex misses Palace fried rice.”

The sound of a door closing. Then quiet.

The melody Reza made kept flowing from the small music player.
In Jakarta's sky, which tonight decided to be kind, one or two stars could be seen among the city lights that never truly died.
Twenty-three years.
Not twenty-three years without wounds. Not without nights when everything felt too heavy. Not without a crack that had briefly felt unmendable.
But twenty-three years chosen — every day, every morning, every small moment where both could choose not to continue but chose to stay.
Kintsugi.
The beauty of a crack's trace mended not by hiding it, but by celebrating it — acknowledging that this once cracked, this once nearly shattered, and that was exactly what made it strong.

Rahmawati was closing her office for the night, preparing tomorrow's client schedule.
Hendri was having dinner with his daughter, now in her sixth semester.
Pak Darmawan was replying to an email from a former student announcing she'd just gotten married — twenty-four years old, already working, already had savings, already ready.

And in thousands of other homes scattered across this archipelago — small conversations were happening. About expectations. About readiness. About the right to say no or say not yet or say: I want to, but the right way.
Conversations that four years ago had no legal foundation. Now they did.
The seed planted — was growing.
Not perfectly. Not uniformly. Not according to plan in every corner.

“Za.”
“Hm?”

The melody flowed.
The city lights sparkled.

No storm lasts forever.
But there's a light that needs no storm to exist.
That light is here.
Has always been here.
